The snow gave way beneath their boots, and they went down hard against the white slope. For one breath there was only the hiss of wind and the frantic beat of their own heart.

Then the wolves closed in.

The first one lunged—not with a roar, but with a sharp, breathless snarl—and its jaws clamped around their forearm. The bite was impossibly sudden: pressure first, crushing and absolute, followed by a bright, tearing pain that seemed to flare all the way to the shoulder. Their fingers went numb almost at once, but the wound itself burned.

Warmth spread beneath the torn sleeve. Blood slipped over their skin in a startling rush, hot enough to feel unreal against the killing cold. It steamed faintly in the air, a red contrast to the snow, while the rest of their body shuddered beneath the wind. The wolf’s breath rolled over them, damp and animal-warm; its teeth held fast as if the arm were caught in an iron trap.

They could feel the cold trying to claim everything—their fingertips, their face, the breath in their lungs—while the blood pulsed hot between the wolf’s teeth and their skin. For a moment, the two sensations met there: winter pressing inward, heat spilling out, neither willing to yield.

The rain on New Carthage fell upward.

It streamed from the pavement in silver threads, pulled toward the storm turbines hanging beneath the city’s floating districts. In the reflection of a broken advertisement, bounty hunter Mara Venn saw her target slip through the alley ahead: a narrow figure in a white coat, one hand clamped around a stolen data cylinder.

“Renn Vale,” Mara called. “By authority of the Interplanetary Claims Office, you’re under arrest.”

Vale glanced back. “You always announce yourself?”

“It saves time.”

“It didn’t save yours.”

He fired a compact pulse pistol. The shot struck the wall beside Mara’s head and burst into blue sparks. She rolled behind a cargo hauler as the alley filled with the smell of hot metal.

Her wrist display flashed three warnings.

**TARGET: ARMED.**
**TARGET: HOSTILE.**
**TARGET: DO NOT ALLOW ESCAPE.**

Mara rose and fired her restraint line. The filament snapped across the alley, but Vale caught it around his forearm and yanked. The sudden force pulled her from cover. He slammed into her, driving her shoulder against the hauler.

For a moment, they struggled in the rain.

Vale was stronger than he looked. His elbow struck her ribs. Mara’s vision flashed white. He reached for the pistol at her hip, fingers closing around its grip.

She released it.

Vale looked surprised.

Mara’s other hand held the weapon she had been waiting to use: a black, palm-sized stun emitter. Its warning ring glowed amber.

“Last chance,” she said.

Vale bared his teeth and lunged.

Mara pressed the emitter against the armored plate over his chest and triggered it.

The weapon gave a sharp, insect-like crack.

Electricity leapt through Vale’s body in a web of blue-white light. His muscles contracted all at once—not like a voluntary movement, but as if invisible hands had seized every limb. His shoulders locked, his fingers curled, and his knees buckled beneath him. The current disrupted the signals traveling between his brain and muscles, overwhelming the nerves that controlled movement. For several seconds, he could neither pull away nor coordinate his body.

A strangled breath escaped him. The shock did not simply hurt; it stole control. His muscles tightened violently, making it difficult to inhale, while the sudden pain and disorientation scattered his thoughts. His heart continued beating, but irregular electrical interference made the weapon dangerous, especially near the chest. Mara’s emitter was calibrated to pulse in brief bursts, enough to disable without sustaining the current.

She released the trigger.

Vale collapsed onto the wet pavement, conscious but unable to rise. His limbs trembled with residual spasms. He dragged in a ragged breath, blinking rain from his eyes.

Mara crouched beside him and snapped a restraint cuff around his wrist. The cuff tightened automatically, projecting a blue field that dampened muscle impulses and prevented tampering.

“You could have just surrendered,” she said.

Vale tried to answer, but his jaw shook too badly.

“I’ll take that as agreement.”

She searched his coat, recovered the data cylinder, and hauled him upright. His legs wobbled beneath him, so she kept one hand on his shoulder while the cuff stabilized his nervous system. The worst of the shock had passed, but the aftereffects remained: weakness, numbness, aching muscles, and a deep, involuntary shiver.

Above them, the floating city groaned as its turbines adjusted altitude.

Vale looked at the glowing towers reflected in the puddles. “You hunters get better weapons every year.”

Mara guided him toward the waiting skiff.

“No,” she said. “Just better targets.”

Her wrist display flashed three warnings.

TARGET: ARMED.
TARGET: HOSTILE.
TARGET: DO NOT ALLOW ESCAPE.

Mara rose and fired her restraint line. The filament snapped across the alley, but Vale caught it around his forearm and yanked. The sudden force pulled her from cover. He slammed into her, driving her shoulder against the hauler.

For a moment, they struggled in the rain.

Vale was stronger than he looked. His elbow struck her ribs. Mara’s vision flashed white. He reached for the pistol at her hip, fingers closing around its grip.

She released it.

Vale looked surprised.

Mara’s other hand held the weapon she had been waiting to use: a black, palm-sized stun emitter. Its warning ring glowed amber.

“Last chance,” she said.

Vale bared his teeth and lunged.

Mara pressed the emitter against the armored plate over his chest and triggered it.

The weapon gave a sharp, insect-like crack.

Electricity leapt through Vale’s body in a web of blue-white light. His muscles contracted all at once—not like a voluntary movement, but as if invisible hands had seized every limb. His shoulders locked, his fingers curled, and his knees buckled beneath him. The current disrupted the signals traveling between his brain and muscles, overwhelming the nerves that controlled movement. For several seconds, he could neither pull away nor coordinate his body.

A strangled breath escaped him. The shock did not simply hurt; it stole control. His muscles tightened violently, making it difficult to inhale, while the sudden pain and disorientation scattered his thoughts. His heart continued beating, but irregular electrical interference made the weapon dangerous, especially near the chest. Mara’s emitter was calibrated to pulse in brief bursts, enough to disable without sustaining the current.

She released the trigger.

Vale collapsed onto the wet pavement, conscious but unable to rise. His limbs trembled with residual spasms. He dragged in a ragged breath, blinking rain from his eyes.

Mara crouched beside him and snapped a restraint cuff around his wrist. The cuff tightened automatically, projecting a blue field that dampened muscle impulses and prevented tampering.

“You could have just surrendered,” she said.

Vale tried to answer, but his jaw shook too badly.

“I’ll take that as agreement.”

She searched his coat, recovered the data cylinder, and hauled him upright. His legs wobbled beneath him, so she kept one hand on his shoulder while the cuff stabilized his nervous system. The worst of the shock had passed, but the aftereffects remained: weakness, numbness, aching muscles, and a deep, involuntary shiver.

Vale looked at the glowing towers reflected in the puddles. “You hunters get better weapons every year.”

Mara guided him toward the waiting skiff.

“No,” she said. “Just better targets.”

Mara woke to the sound of a clock counting down.

At first, she thought the numbers were inside her head. Then the red digits came into focus above her: **09:58**. A speaker crackled, and a calm recorded voice explained the rules. The lock around her wrist would not open until she paid the required price. The instrument placed within reach was not described in detail. It didn’t need to be.

For several seconds, Mara simply stared at it.

Her mind rejected the room in layers—the concrete walls, the drain in the floor, the metal band biting into her skin. She searched for loopholes with the frantic precision of someone trying to wake from a nightmare. Maybe the voice was bluffing. Maybe the mechanism was faulty. Maybe someone was watching and would intervene before the countdown reached zero.

Then the clock changed.

**08:41.**

The denial collapsed.

Mara tugged against the restraint until the edges of the cuff burned. Pain came quickly, cleanly, and uselessly. She stopped before she wasted her strength. Across from her, a dark pane of glass reflected a stranger: pale, shaking, breathing too fast.

“No,” she whispered.

The word sounded childish in the empty room.

She tried bargaining next. With the speaker. With whoever had built the trap. With God, though she hadn’t prayed in years. She promised anything—confessions, money, obedience, a better life—while knowing the room had been designed to make promises meaningless.

At **06:12**, she began to prepare.

Not for the act itself, not yet. For the moment before it.

She planted her feet against the floor and tested the range of her free hand. She rolled her shoulders, forcing air into her lungs in slow counts. Her fingers trembled so badly that she clasped them together and held them still. Every movement felt like a betrayal: arranging herself, checking the restraint, making sure she would not lose consciousness too soon.

The worst part was the deliberateness. The trap demanded that she participate. It wanted her to become the person who chose the pain, even though the choice had been forced upon her.

Mara looked again at the clock.

**04:03.**

She closed her eyes and pictured her brother’s kitchen, sunlight on the counter, a chipped blue mug beside the sink. Ordinary things. Things that belonged to a world where pain was accidental and help arrived when someone called for it.

When she opened her eyes, she was still shaking—but she was breathing evenly now.

“I am not what you made me do,” she said to the camera.

The speaker remained silent.

At **01:00**, she reached forward. Her hand hovered there, suspended between terror and necessity. She thought of stopping. She thought of surrender. She thought of the cold, impersonal certainty of the clock continuing without her permission.

Then she gripped the instrument, not looking at it, and braced herself.

The final seconds disappeared one by one.

Mara turned her face away, fixed her eyes on the blue mug in her memory, and acted.

The room filled with her cry.

The sea was calm in the way a blade was calm—flat, bright, and waiting.

Captain Vey stood at the end of the deck with one hand resting on the hilt of her cutlass. Behind her, the crew had formed a silent ring around Tomas, the mutineer. His wrists were bound, and his boots scraped uselessly against the planks as two sailors marched him toward the narrow board jutting over the ship’s side.

Below, the sharks had already gathered.

Their dark fins cut slow circles through the blue water. Every so often, one rolled beneath the surface, revealing a pale flash of belly before vanishing into the depths. There were six of them. Perhaps more. Tomas counted twice and lost track when one surfaced directly beneath the plank.

“No,” he whispered.

The word passed through the watching crew like a gust of wind, but no one answered.

Captain Vey stepped closer. “You raised steel against your captain.”

“I was afraid,” Tomas said. His voice cracked. “We all were. The storm, the navy—”

“You were afraid,” she said, “and decided the rest of us should pay for it.”

The plank creaked as Tomas was forced onto it. It extended only a few feet beyond the rail, narrow enough that his boots hung over the water on either side. Spray leapt up from the waves and struck his face. Far below, the sharks continued their circling, patient as clock hands.

He looked down.

The water seemed impossibly far away. The sun glimmered on the surface, turning the sea into a field of broken glass, but between the flashes he saw shapes moving—long, gray bodies, fins, open mouths glimpsed and gone.

His knees began to tremble.

“Captain,” he pleaded.

Vey’s expression did not change, but her voice lowered. “You were given mercy once.”

“I’ll work. I’ll scrub the decks. I’ll—”

“You’ll take three steps,” she said. “And you’ll remember, with every one, what you asked the crew to risk.”

The sailor behind him gave a shove.

Tomas stumbled forward. One step.

A shark rose beneath him, close enough that its shadow swallowed the plank. He cried out and flung his arms wide. The crew watched as he fought to keep his balance, toes curling over the edge.

“Two,” called Captain Vey.

Tomas turned his head. “Please!”

The ocean breathed below him. Another fin sliced across the water, then another, tightening the circle.

“Three.”

He froze.

For a heartbeat, the only sound was the creaking ship and the soft slap of waves against the hull. Tomas’s face had gone white. Tears cut clean lines through the salt on his cheeks, and his bound hands shook so violently that the rope rattled.

Captain Vey lifted one finger.

The sailor behind Tomas stepped forward.

With a strangled cry, the mutineer jumped—not into the sea, but backward, scrambling onto the deck. He collapsed at the captain’s boots, sobbing.

Vey looked down at him for a long moment. Then she turned to the crew.

“Untie him,” she said.

The sailors stared.

“He will live,” the captain continued, “but he will spend the voyage in irons, hauling lines under guard. Let every man aboard understand this: fear is no excuse for betrayal. And the next mutineer who reaches that plank will not be pulled back.”

Below, the sharks circled once more, disappointed, before sinking into the dark water.

Tomas kept his eyes shut as the crew dragged him away. But even with the deck beneath him and the ropes cut from his wrists, he could still feel the plank swaying under his feet—and see the patient shapes waiting below.

The first thing she noticed was the pressure.

Something hard and unfamiliar was cinched against her ribs, tight enough to make each breath feel borrowed. Beneath the straps, wires scratched and shifted with every tremor of her body—thin, cold lines against her skin, some taped flat, others trembling loose like veins pulled out of place.

Then she heard it.

Tick.

Her breath caught.

Tick. Tick.

The sound seemed impossibly loud, louder than the alarms, louder than the pounding of her heart. It came from the device pressed to her chest, steady and patient, counting down to something she could not imagine without seeing flashes of light and pieces of herself scattered across the floor.

“No,” she whispered.

Her fingers hovered over the wires, afraid to touch them, afraid even to let them remain where they were. Sweat gathered beneath the straps and made the casing slip against her shirt. Every tiny movement tugged at the tape. Every tug sent a jolt of panic through her.

Tick.

She tried to breathe slowly. In. Out.

But the straps seemed to tighten with her lungs. Her vision narrowed. The room tilted at the edges, faces blurring into pale shapes and open mouths. Someone was saying her name, but the voice sounded distant, underwater.

“Get it off,” she gasped. “Get it off me.”

Tick. Tick.

Her hands began to shake violently. She clutched them against her sides, then tore them away, terrified that either motion might trigger something. The wires brushed her knuckles, soft as thread and just as menacing. She imagined them snapping. Imagined the ticking speeding up. Imagined the silence that would come afterward.

“No, no, no—”

Her voice broke into a sob. She backed into the wall, the device digging harder into her sternum, and slid halfway down it before someone caught her shoulders.

“Don’t touch me!” she screamed.

The ticking continued, calm and indifferent, while her hysteria climbed higher and higher around it, until the whole world seemed reduced to three things: the pressure on her chest, the wires against her skin, and that merciless little sound.

The power had gone out sometime after midnight.

Mara woke to the refrigerator clicking off and the sudden, total silence that followed. For a few seconds she lay still, listening to the house settle around her. Rain tapped against the bedroom window. Somewhere downstairs, a drop of water struck metal with a slow, deliberate ping.

She reached for her phone.

The screen lit her face blue. No service. Twelve percent battery.

Then she heard it again.

A soft scrape from the hallway.

Mara sat up.

“Ben?”

No answer.

Her husband was away for work, but she had almost called his name anyway. The mistake hung in the dark, embarrassing and loud.

She slid out of bed. The floorboards were cold beneath her feet. Her phone’s flashlight threw a narrow cone across the room, catching the edge of the dresser, the open closet door, the brass hook where her robe hung. Everything looked ordinary.

The hallway did not.

At the far end, the bathroom door stood half open. Mara was certain she had closed it before bed.

She took one step toward it.

The old house creaked beneath her.

Behind her, in the darkness beside the wardrobe, someone held their breath.

Mara stopped.

Rain hissed against the glass. She lifted the phone, sweeping the light across the room. The beam passed over the bed, the chair piled with clothes, the curtains shifting faintly at the window.

It did not reach the space between the wardrobe and the wall.

Nothing moved there.

She told herself that was good. Nothing moving was good.

Then the bathroom tap began to drip.

Mara backed into the hallway. Her shoulder brushed the doorframe. She flinched at the contact and nearly dropped the phone. The beam wobbled across the runner carpet and landed on a dark smear near the stairs.

Mud.

A footprint.

She stared at it.

Another print showed on the next step.

The front door was downstairs. The kitchen phone was downstairs. Her keys were downstairs.

The bedroom door was behind her.

She turned toward the stairs, keeping her phone pointed ahead. The light barely reached the bottom. Shadows filled the gaps between the banisters, thick and still.

One step.

The house gave a low groan.

Two.

Mara gripped the railing. Her breathing had become shallow, noiseless little pulls. She could hear the rain, the tap, the faint electrical buzz of her phone.

On the third step, something shifted below.

She froze.

A shape stood at the foot of the stairs.

Not a shadow. A person.

Mara’s phone light swept downward, catching a shoulder, the pale oval of a hand, the glint of metal.

The figure stepped back before the beam found their face.

Mara made a sound that was almost a scream and stumbled upward. Her heel struck the edge of the step. She fell against the wall, phone flying from her hand.

It landed below, screen-up.

For one terrible moment, the flashlight pointed directly beneath the stairs.

The intruder was there now, crouched in the narrow space, watching her.

The knife in their hand reflected the phone’s cold light.

Mara scrambled backward, palms sliding over the wallpaper. The bedroom was only a few feet away. She could reach the door. She could slam it. Lock it.

The figure rose.

Slowly. Carefully.

Mara turned and ran.

She hit the bedroom door with her shoulder, caught the handle, and yanked. The door swung inward. She threw herself across the room, searching blindly for the window latch.

Behind her, footsteps entered the hall.

Not hurried.

That was the worst of it. Whoever was coming knew she had nowhere to go.

Mara found the window and pushed. It stuck. She shoved again, harder, making the frame rattle.

The footsteps stopped outside the bedroom.

She looked back.

The doorway was empty.

Her hands slipped from the latch.

In the black mirror of the window, she saw the room behind her—and the figure standing just inside the door.

The knife hung at their side.

Mara held her breath.

So did the person behind her.

The rain continued tapping at the glass, patient as fingers.

Mud.

A footprint.

She stared at it.

Another print showed on the next step.

The front door was downstairs. The kitchen phone was downstairs. Her keys were downstairs.

The bedroom door was behind her.

She turned toward the stairs, keeping her phone pointed ahead. The light barely reached the bottom. Shadows filled the gaps between the banisters, thick and still.

One step.

The house gave a low groan.

Two.

Mara gripped the railing. Her breathing had become shallow, noiseless little pulls. She could hear the rain, the tap, the faint electrical buzz of her phone.

On the third step, something shifted below.

She froze.

A shape stood at the foot of the stairs.

Not a shadow. A person.

Mara’s phone light swept downward, catching a shoulder, the pale oval of a hand, the glint of metal.

The figure stepped back before the beam found their face.

Mara made a sound that was almost a scream and stumbled upward. Her heel struck the edge of the step. She fell against the wall, phone flying from her hand.

It landed below, screen-up.

For one terrible moment, the flashlight pointed directly beneath the stairs.

The intruder was there now, crouched in the narrow space, watching her.

The knife in their hand reflected the phone’s cold light.

Mara scrambled backward, palms sliding over the wallpaper. The bedroom was only a few feet away. She could reach the door. She could slam it. Lock it.

The figure rose.

Slowly. Carefully.

Mara turned and ran.

She hit the bedroom door with her shoulder, caught the handle, and yanked. The door swung inward. She threw herself across the room, searching blindly for the window latch.

Behind her, footsteps entered the hall.

Not hurried.

That was the worst of it. Whoever was coming knew she had nowhere to go.

Mara found the window and pushed. It stuck. She shoved again, harder, making the frame rattle.

The footsteps stopped outside the bedroom.

She looked back.

The doorway was empty.

Her hands slipped from the latch.

In the black mirror of the window, she saw the room behind her—and the figure standing just inside the door.

The knife hung at their side.

Mara held her breath.

So did the person behind her.

The rain continued tapping at the glass, patient as fingers.

The gas reached him before he saw it—a pale, oily haze sinking into the trench and pooling along the sandbags. At first, it seemed only to sting. His eyes watered. His nose ran. Then his throat closed around the next breath.

He bent double, clawing at his collar as if he could tear open a passage for air. Each inhale came in thin, ragged pulls and ended in a wet, tearing cough. His lungs felt scalded from the inside. He coughed until his ribs cramped, until strings of saliva hung from his mouth, until every breath became a desperate gamble that produced almost no oxygen. A harsh wheeze rattled deep in his chest, followed by the awful sensation of fluid gathering where air should have been.

His eyes burned so fiercely that the trench blurred into streaks of mud and gray light. Tears streamed down his face, mixing with grime. His skin prickled, then burned. He stumbled against the wall, fingers digging into packed earth, but his legs had begun to tremble beneath him. His heart hammered wildly—not from exertion, but from the animal terror of suffocation.

His mind narrowed with his airway. Training, orders, names—all of it fell away. There was only the next breath. The next breath. The next.

He tried to call for help, but his voice emerged as a shredded croak. Panic surged when he realized he could no longer draw enough air to shout. He imagined his lungs collapsing, imagined drowning while standing upright. The thought was irrational and absolute. He tore at his mask, then fumbled to replace it, hands clumsy and numb with fear.

Around him, the trench had become a nightmare of sound: coughing, retching, boots scraping through mud, men calling for medics in voices that broke apart halfway through the words. Someone was praying. Someone else was vomiting. The gas hissed softly through the chaos.

His vision began to pulse at the edges. Blackness crept inward. He felt strangely detached, as if he were watching another man suffer—watching that man crouch in the mud, shoulders jerking, mouth open in a silent plea for air.

Then came the worst sensation: the false relief of a breath that seemed to fill his chest, followed by the realization that it had not been enough. His body convulsed, demanding oxygen. His lungs gurgled and seized. He scraped at the ground, trying to pull himself toward clearer air, but his strength drained away in shuddering waves.

The last thing he understood was that breathing had become labor, pain, and terror—each breath a battle he was steadily losing.

The rain silvered the windows of Don Vescari’s office, turning the city beyond them into a blur of headlights and smoke.

Vescari sat behind his desk, one hand resting on a closed ledger. Across from him, Nico stood with his coat still damp from the weather.

“Sit,” the Don said.

Nico took the chair.

Vescari opened the ledger and ran a finger down the page. “Mara Bellini.”

Nico said nothing.

“She was paid to keep quiet.”

“She was.”

“She was paid to keep the books clean.”

“She did.”

Vescari looked up. “And then she spoke to the wrong people.”

Nico’s jaw tightened. “That’s what we’ve heard.”

“No,” Vescari said. “That’s what she told them.”

The room settled into silence. Somewhere downstairs, a glass broke, followed by a muffled laugh.

Vescari closed the ledger.

“Your brother trusted her.”

“My brother trusted too many people.”

“Your brother is dead.”

Nico lowered his eyes.

The Don leaned back in his chair. “Mara has mistaken a warning for a negotiation. She thinks distance makes her untouchable.”

“Where is she?”

“Outside the city. A little house near the lake. She believes the water is between her and her mistakes.”

Nico waited.

Vescari picked up a silver letter opener and turned it slowly between his fingers. “Bring her home.”

“And if she refuses?”

“Then make other arrangements.”

Nico’s gaze lifted. “You want it quiet.”

“I want it finished.” Vescari set the letter opener down. “No spectacle. No message. No one hears her name again unless they’re reading it on a stone.”

Nico nodded once.

“Take Sal,” the Don continued. “He knows how to close a door without making a draft.”

“And the body?”

Vescari’s expression did not change. “The lake has kept our secrets before.”

Nico rose.

At the door, Vescari spoke again.

“Nico.”

He turned.

“Do not confuse this with revenge.”

“What is it, then?”

“Maintenance.”

The Don reopened his ledger, already finished with the matter.

“See that the business remains healthy.”

When he tried to stand, his knees failed him. He caught the edge of the table, upsetting the silver spoon, and sank heavily against the carpet.

She was beside him at once.

His skin was clammy beneath her fingers. Sweat beaded his brow and gathered at his temples, while his hands shook with small, uncontrollable tremors. He drew breath in short, shallow pulls. Each seemed to catch halfway down, followed by a dry, strangled cough.

Then his grip released.

For a moment there was only the ticking clock, the dying fire, and the dark stain soaking slowly into the carpet.

The arena lights snapped on at noon, bleaching the concrete white and turning every face in the ration stands into a pale mask.

Above the gates, the Ministry’s seal rotated on a giant screen:

**ONE VICTOR. TWO WEEKS OF FOOD.**

Mara tightened her grip on the scavenged spear. Across the dust, Joren stood with a length of pipe in both hands. They had grown up in the same ration queue, years ago, before the Ministry began drawing names from the lottery drum. His younger sister was somewhere behind the eastern glass, watching. Mara knew because Joren kept glancing toward that section.

The bell sounded.

Joren charged.

Their weapons struck with a crack that shuddered up Mara’s arms. He swung again, wild and desperate. She gave ground, boots sliding through grit, until her back nearly touched the arena wall. The crowd began to chant—not his name or hers, but the word printed on every ration card:

“EAT. EAT. EAT.”

Joren lunged.

Mara twisted aside. The pipe scraped across her ribs, tearing cloth and skin. Pain flashed hot beneath her breath. Joren stumbled past her, and for one suspended moment they stood shoulder to shoulder, both staring at the weapon in her hands.

He turned first.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

Mara saw the apology in his face, and the fear beneath it. He raised the pipe.

She moved before he could.

The spear drove into the space beneath his ribs with a blunt, heavy impact. His breath left him in a small, startled sound. Mara felt the resistance give, felt the shaft jolt in her palms. She caught him as his knees folded, lowering him rather than letting him crash onto the concrete.

Mara found the brake lines beneath Calder’s car just before dawn, silver in the weak garage light.

For three years, she had told herself that Calder’s death would be justice. He had falsified the inspection reports that condemned her brother’s factory, then lied under oath when the machinery failed. Her brother had died in the collapse; Calder had walked away with a promotion and a polished reputation.

Mara held the tool in her hand and listened to the rain ticking against the roof.

He deserves to be afraid, she thought. He deserves to lose the easy future he stole. The thought hardened into something colder: If he dies, no one else can be hurt by him. One ruined life to balance the scale. One act of violence to end the consequences of his.

For a moment, revenge felt less like hatred than arithmetic.

Then she imagined Calder’s daughter in the passenger seat, trusting her father to bring her home. Mara saw, with terrible clarity, how easily justice could become another name for making strangers suffer.

She lowered the tool.

Instead, she photographed the evidence, sent it anonymously to the police, and left the car untouched. Calder was arrested two days later—not for the collapse, at least not yet, but for attempting to murder his business partner, whose brakes he had already sabotaged.

Mara never learned whether the police believed her evidence. But she understood something she hadn’t before: wanting someone punished was not the same as wanting to become the person who decided how much they should suffer.

Only the flies, industrious,  
keep up their small, unending strain.

not sleeping, though the earth is deep;

and will not let the silence sleep.

The dog came out of the dust like it had been thrown there—ribs showing, fur clotted with mud, one ear hanging by a ragged fold. It saw the scrap in Mara’s hand and forgot its fear.

So did she.

The meat was no bigger than her thumb, a strip torn from a can she’d found beneath the ruins. She had held it under her tongue for an hour, letting the salt and grease spread through her mouth, pretending it was a meal. Now the dog lunged.

Its teeth caught her sleeve and drove her backward. Mara hit the concrete hard enough to knock the breath from her chest. The scrap flew between them. The dog snapped at it, missed, and turned on her instead.

She jammed her forearm across its throat. The animal bucked beneath her, all bone and desperate strength. Its claws raked her coat. Heat flashed across her skin as teeth found the meat of her arm—not deep, but deep enough. Mara screamed and slammed the heel of her hand against its skull.

Once.

Twice.

The dog loosened its grip. She rolled away, clutching her arm, but the animal was already crawling toward the food. It dragged one hind leg behind it. Its breath came in wet, frantic bursts. For a second they stared at each other: two starving creatures measuring the distance between hunger and death.

Then it lunged again.

Mara caught it by the neck and drove it into the rubble. The dog twisted, snarling, its jaws snapping inches from her face. She could smell rot on its breath. She could feel every rib moving beneath her hands. It fought not from rage but from the same hollow command beating inside her: eat, or stop.

She struck until the struggle went slack.

For a long moment, Mara stayed crouched over it, shaking. The world narrowed to the blood on her sleeve, the pounding in her ears, and the scrap of meat lying in the dust.

She picked it up.

It was gritty with sand. She swallowed it anyway.

The shot had gone in just below Mara’s ribs.

She was on her back in the mud, one hand clamped over the wound, the other pawing weakly at the rain. Blood seeped between her fingers in dark, glossy sheets.

“Get it out,” she gasped.

Jonas stared at her. “I’m not a surgeon.”

“You’re the closest thing we have.”

The others were gone—dead, scattered, or running toward the sound of the approaching patrol. Behind them, the woods flashed white with muzzle fire. Every report seemed to make Mara’s body jerk beneath him.

He had a knife. He had a bottle of whiskey.

That was all.

Jonas dragged her beneath the ruined stone wall and tore open her shirt. The bullet had punched through skin and muscle, leaving a ragged black-edged hole beneath her ribs. Blood welled with every breath. When she inhaled, the wound made a wet, sucking sound.

“No,” he whispered.

Mara caught his sleeve. Her grip was astonishingly strong. “If you leave it, I die.”

“You might die if I don’t.”

“Then do something useful.”

His hands shook so badly he nearly dropped the bottle. He poured whiskey over the blade. It ran off in amber streams, carrying flecks of dirt and blood into the grass.

Mara saw the knife and began to sob.

“Don’t look at it,” he said.

“I’m looking at you.”

He poured whiskey over the wound.

She screamed.

The sound seemed too large for her body. Her back arched off the ground, heels digging furrows in the mud. For a moment Jonas thought she had stopped breathing. Then she sucked in air with a broken, rattling gasp.

“It burns,” she choked.

“I know.”

“You don’t know anything.”

He pressed his palm around the wound. Blood flooded hot between his fingers. Somewhere inside her, something bubbled when she breathed.

The bullet had not gone through. He could feel it—or thought he could—buried under torn muscle. He had seen field medics do this once, years ago, under a bridge. He remembered the certainty of their hands. The calm voices. The clean instruments.

He had none of those things.

Only the knife.

“Bite down,” he said.

Mara laughed once, wildly. “On what?”

He shoved the neck of the whiskey bottle toward her. She clamped her teeth around it.

The first flare of orange gave him a jolt that felt almost like relief. After weeks of paperwork, rehearsed explanations, and the dull pressure of debt, the fire was vivid—honest in a way nothing else had been. It moved without asking permission, climbing through the abandoned warehouse and turning every dark window into an eye.

He watched, transfixed. The old beams cracked; glass burst inward; shadows leapt across the walls. He told himself the building was already worthless, already condemned, already empty of anything that mattered. That made it easier not to think about the rooms that had once held people, or the workers who had depended on the place, or the lives that might be disrupted by the smoke and sirens.

The flames seemed to reward him for letting go. They erased the evidence of his failures as quickly as they consumed the walls. For a few reckless minutes, he felt powerful—not because he had built anything, but because he could decide what remained.

Then the heat reached him, and beneath the thrill came a colder realization: the fire did not care about his plan. It would not stop at the warehouse, or obey the story he had invented for the insurance company. It only spread, indifferent to guilt, money, and excuses.

**Torturer:** You’ve been here six hours. The door opens, the clock moves, and still you say nothing.

**Captive:** I’ve said everything I know.

**Torturer:** No. You’ve said everything you think will keep you comfortable.

**Captive:** If I knew the password, I’d give it to you.

**Torturer:** That’s the first lie you told tonight.

**Captive:** Then why are you still asking?

**Torturer:** Because I’m offering you a choice. You can give me the password now, while your fear is still doing most of the work. Or you can wait until fear is no longer enough.

**Captive:** You expect me to believe you’ll let me go?

**Torturer:** I expect you to understand that I don’t need you to believe me. I only need you to decide which pain you can live with: the pain of speaking, or the pain of making me prove I’m serious.

**Captive:** You think threatening me makes you powerful?

**Torturer:** No. The fact that you’re watching the clock makes me powerful.

**Captive:** I’m not watching it.

**Torturer:** You looked at it seventeen times.

**Captive:** You’re counting?

**Torturer:** I’m counting everything. Your breaths. The pauses before you answer. The way your hands tighten whenever I mention the server room.

**Captive:** You don’t know anything about me.

**Torturer:** I know you’re trying to convince yourself that silence is still a strategy. It was, earlier. Now it’s only postponement.

**Captive:** Suppose I give you a password. What stops you from hurting me anyway?

**Torturer:** Nothing. That’s why you should have spoken before you asked that question.

**Captive:** Then there’s no reason to trust you.

**Torturer:** Trust has nothing to do with it. This is arithmetic. One word now, and the night ends. One more refusal, and the cost rises. You don’t need to trust me. You only need to believe I’m patient.

**Captive:** And if the password doesn’t work?

**Torturer:** Then we’ll both learn something. But if you give me the wrong one deliberately, I’ll know. That will be worse than silence.

**Captive:** You keep saying “worse” as if the word itself is supposed to break me.

**Torturer:** Words are useful. They let the imagination do the work before I have to.

**Captive:** You’re a coward.

**Torturer:** Perhaps. But you’re still afraid of what a coward might do.

**Captive:** Go to hell.

**Torturer:** In a moment. First, I’m going to leave this room for five minutes. When I come back, the lamp will be on, the restraints will be tighter, and you’ll have one final chance to give me the password before we stop talking.

**Captive:** And if I don’t?

**Torturer:** Then you’ll discover how long five minutes can feel when you know they’re the last peaceful ones you’re going to have.

**Captive:** You think I’ll break?

**Torturer:** Everyone breaks. The only question is whether you choose the shape of it.

**Captive:** …

**Torturer:** The password.

**Captive:** I don’t know it.

**Torturer:** That was your last peaceful answer.

Smoke poured beneath the door before the flames ever appeared.

Mara coughed once, then doubled over as the air scraped through her throat. The room blurred around her, gray turning black at the edges. Somewhere below, glass shattered. The fire had reached the first floor.

“Vale,” she rasped. “You did this.”

Her rival’s words echoed in her memory: *If I can’t bring you down, I’ll bury you.*

Heat rolled up the stairwell in waves. It pressed against her face, dried the moisture from her eyes, and made every breath feel like swallowing ash. She pulled her sleeve over her mouth, but the fabric only trapped the smoke against her skin. Her lungs seized. Panic surged through her faster than the fire.

The window.

Mara stumbled toward it, one hand against the wall for balance. The floorboards shuddered beneath her boots. She reached the window and threw the latch, but the frame had swollen shut. She struck it with her palm. Once. Twice.

Nothing.

A burst of flame climbed the curtains behind her.

She screamed and hurled herself against the glass. It cracked but didn’t break. Heat snapped across her back. Her coat began to smolder, and beneath it, her skin prickled—then blistered. She slapped at the fabric, choking as the pain sharpened into something bright and unbearable.

The ceiling groaned.

Mara dropped to her knees, crawling now, because the air near the floor was only slightly less poisonous. Her fingers found the doorjamb. She dragged herself toward the hall, but fire bloomed beyond the doorway, turning the corridor into a furnace.

No way out.

Her vision narrowed. Her chest convulsed, fighting for air that wasn’t there. She clawed at the floorboards, nails splitting, tears streaming down her soot-blackened cheeks.

Then she heard it.

A faint metallic scrape beneath the floor.

Mara froze.

Again: scrape… scrape… scrape.

The old building’s plans flashed through her mind. A service tunnel beneath the east wing, sealed decades ago. Vale had known about it. He had once told her the passage was impossible to open.

Something struck the boards from below.

A narrow plank sprang upward, vomiting smoke into the room. Mara recoiled as a hand—burned, trembling, unmistakably human—reached through the gap and groped blindly across the floor.

Her heart lurched.

“Help me,” a voice whispered from beneath the burning house.

Mara stared at the hand as the ceiling above her began to collapse.

Then the stranger caught her wrist—and pulled.

The rifle lay in the case like a question nobody wanted answered.

I opened it slow. No drama in the motion, no wasted flourish. Drama was for witnesses, and witnesses were a luxury I couldn’t afford. The metal caught the weak yellow light, cold and clean, pretending it had never been near a human decision.

I checked the pieces the way a priest checks his scripture. Stock. Barrel. Glass. Magazine. Each one had its place. Each one clicked home with the quiet confidence of machinery built by men who’d never have to look into the eyes of the person it was meant for.

That was the trick of the job: reduce a soul to components.

The client called the target a problem. The target called himself innocent. Both men were probably lying. Most people were. The difference was that one of them had money, and the other had a price on his head.

I ran a cloth along the metal, though it didn’t need cleaning. My hands needed the work. They needed something simple to do while the mind wandered into darker rooms.

You tell yourself morality is a luxury. You tell yourself the world is already cruel, and all you’re doing is choosing where the cruelty lands. You tell yourself there are worse men than you.

Then, if you’re lucky, you stop listening before the excuses start sounding like prayers.

The rifle came together in silence. Not perfectly—nothing ever does—but sufficiently. That was the word men like me used when we wanted to sleep afterward. Sufficiently.

Outside, the city dragged itself through the night, coughing light through the blinds. Somewhere beyond the buildings, the target was eating dinner, laughing at something, believing tomorrow belonged to him.

I wondered if he had a daughter. A dog. A drawer full of old receipts and photographs. I wondered whether knowing those things would make the job harder, or merely make me better at lying about it.

The case stood open at my feet. The rifle rested across my knees, heavy with consequence and empty of opinion.

Machines don’t make choices. People do.

That was the part nobody paid me to carry.

I closed the case, leaving the final decision where it had always been—not in the steel, not in the scope, not in the trembling dark beyond the window, but in the hand that reached for it.

Rainwater threaded through the alley’s broken pavement, carrying cigarette ash toward the gutter. Mara kept one hand inside her coat, gripping the envelope. Across from her, Deke stood beneath the flickering security light, his face pale and shiny with sweat.

“You said the money was clean,” he whispered.

“It is.”

“Then why are the sirens getting closer?”

Mara glanced toward the street. Red light pulsed faintly between the buildings.

Deke’s expression collapsed into panic. He lunged for the envelope.

She jerked back, but he caught her sleeve. The paper packet tore between them, and a spill of banknotes fluttered into the puddles. Deke stared down at them for half a second—long enough for Mara to shove him against the brick wall.

He struck it with a grunt. She reached for the remaining cash, but his hand snapped out and caught her wrist. Then he pulled a knife.

The blade appeared so quickly it seemed to materialize from the rain.

Mara froze. Deke’s breathing came fast and ragged.

“Give me the bag,” he said.

“You already have the money.”

“I said the bag.”

He slashed—not cleanly, not with control, but in a frightened arc. Mara twisted aside. The knife scraped her coat and bit into the flesh just below her ribs.

For an instant, she felt nothing but pressure, a hard, hot punch beneath her skin. Then the pain arrived: sharp at the center, spreading outward in waves that tightened her breath. Her side went strangely numb around the cut, while every movement sent a bright, nauseating throb through her body.

She drove her forehead into Deke’s nose.

He staggered, loosening his grip. Mara seized his knife wrist with both hands. They crashed into the wall, boots slipping on wet concrete. Deke tried to wrench free, his elbow striking her shoulder; she felt the impact jar through her teeth. The knife trembled between them, its point wavering inches from her stomach.

“Let go!” he gasped.

Mara twisted his wrist until his fingers opened. The knife clattered onto the pavement.

Deke kicked it away, but Mara hooked her foot behind his ankle and shoved. He fell hard, landing among the scattered bills. For a moment neither of them moved. Rain pattered against the metal fire escape overhead, and the sirens grew louder.

Mara pressed her palm to her side. Warmth seeped between her fingers despite the cold rain. Deke looked at the blood, then at her, and the desperation in his face gave way to something worse: calculation.

He scrambled backward.

Mara picked up the knife.

“Don’t,” she said, though her voice shook.

Deke glanced toward the mouth of the alley and ran. Mara stayed where she was, bent over and breathing through the pain, while the stolen money dissolved into the gutter.

Rain had been working the alley since midnight, turning the brickwork black and the pavement into a shallow, oily river. It ran in threads along the gutters, carrying cigarette ash, pink foam, and the loose grit of the city toward a rusted drain.

Detective Mara Venn stopped beneath the yellow tape and looked in.

The body lay on its back between two overflowing dumpsters, one arm crooked beneath it, the other flung toward the wall as if it had been reaching for an exit. The victim’s coat was dark with rain except where it had opened at the chest. There, the fabric was darker still.

Venn did not step forward immediately. She let the scene settle into its separate facts.

Male. Middle-aged. No identification visible. One deep wound to the throat. Multiple blunt-force injuries to the face. Blood loss substantial. Position inconsistent with the final assault.

The rain had diluted the edges, but not erased them. A fan of blood stained the bricks behind the head, broken by the horizontal lines of mortar. On the ground, beneath the victim’s right shoulder, was a broad smear where someone had dragged him several feet. The heel marks ended near the mouth of the alley. The footprints continued in the opposite direction.

“Camera?” she asked.

Constable Hales stood behind her, pale beneath the blue wash of the patrol lights. “Corner store has one facing the street. This alley’s blind.”

“Everyone says that until they check.”

He nodded and moved off, grateful for the instruction.

Venn pulled on a second pair of gloves over the first. The latex snapped against her wrists. She stepped around a puddle, careful not to disturb the impressions along its edge. The cold had stiffened the body’s fingers. Dirt packed beneath the nails. A crescent of skin was missing from the right index finger.

She crouched.

The face had begun to swell. One eye was sealed shut, the other half-open and fixed on nothing. Rainwater ran from the brow, gathered at the bridge of the nose, and slid into the mouth. The lips were split. There was a coppery smell beneath the wet concrete and sour garbage, faint but persistent, like coins held too long in a closed fist.

Venn leaned closer, not from curiosity but necessity.

The throat wound had been made by a narrow blade. Clean entry. Downward angle. The cut was not ragged enough for a broken bottle, not wide enough for a kitchen knife used carelessly. Whoever had done it had known where to place the steel and had taken the time to finish the movement.

The bruising told a different story.

The victim had been struck before the throat was opened. The left cheek was flattened and darkening. There were two parallel abrasions along the jaw, perhaps from a ring or the edge of a tool. The knuckles of the left hand were scraped raw, suggesting a brief defense. Not much of one.

Venn touched nothing.

A strand of red wool clung to the victim’s coat near the collar. She marked it with a numbered tent card. Beside the body, half-submerged in rainwater, lay a watch with its crystal broken. The hands had stopped at 2:17.

She checked the victim’s pockets. Wallet, empty. No phone. A receipt folded into quarters, the ink blurred beyond recovery. In the inner pocket, a brass key on a strip of blue tape.

“Photographer’s here,” Hales called.

“Good.”

Venn rose. Her knees protested in the cold, but her face remained still.

At the alley entrance, a uniformed officer vomited discreetly behind a squad car. The smell drifted in on the wind: sour stomach, wet wool, diesel exhaust. Venn registered it the way she registered the rain, the blood, and the broken watch. All of it belonged to the scene. None of it belonged to her.

She looked again at the footprints.

Three distinct patterns. The victim’s shoes. A narrow-soled boot with a worn outer heel. And a third print, larger, pressed deep into the mud beside the drag marks.

Two people had come into the alley.

Only one had walked out.

Venn stood beneath the rain and watched the photographer’s flash turn the body white, then red, then white again.

“Bag the key separately,” she said. “And get the medical examiner to look at the bruising before they move him.”

Hales glanced at her. “You think the throat wound wasn’t the cause of death?”

“I think someone wanted us to think it was.”

She stepped back beneath the tape, leaving the dead man to the lights and the weather. The alley continued to drain itself around him, carrying away everything it could—blood, dirt, footprints, the last thin warmth of the night.

They clawed at the wall, stumbled, and called for help, though the sound that came out was thin and strangled.

The building groaned around them. Their vision narrowed. Their skin screamed with every second of exposure, while the desperate need to breathe became the only thing left in the world.

The blast had torn the market out of its rhythm. Stalls leaned at broken angles, their awnings shredded and fluttering in the hot air. Fruit rolled through the dust, crushed beneath fallen baskets and scattered glass. A cooking fire hissed where a gas canister had overturned, sending a thin ribbon of smoke into the sky.

People lay among the wreckage—some motionless beneath collapsed tables, others twisted where the force had thrown them. The living moved carefully between them, calling names, lifting debris with bare hands, pressing cloth against wounds. A child’s shoe rested beside a shattered display of oranges. Somewhere, a phone rang and rang beneath the rubble.

Then, strangely, the market went quiet.

The usual bargaining, engines, laughter, and calls from vendors had vanished. Even the cries of the injured seemed swallowed by the dust. For a few suspended seconds, everyone stood listening to the ringing phone, the faint crackle of fire, and the low, stunned breathing of those still alive.

Afterward, the silence felt heavier than the explosion. It settled over the bodies, the broken stalls, and the empty spaces where people had been, as if the whole market were holding its breath and waiting for the world to explain what had happened.

The yard had gone silent before the first blow.

The prisoner stood with his wrists bound above his head, boots planted in the mud, shoulders trembling from more than the cold. Behind him, the guard drew back the whip. Its braided length whispered through the air, then cracked with a report like a musket shot.

The prisoner jerked against the ropes.

For a moment, nothing moved but the loose end of the lash, shivering where it had struck. Then a dark line appeared across his back, brightening as it opened. His breath came out in a thin, broken gasp.

The second stroke landed lower. The sound was different up close—not only the sharp snap of leather, but the heavy, wet slap that followed as it wrapped around him and tore away. His knees buckled. The ropes creaked overhead.

The office occupied the top floor of a building that had never had a sign.

A wall of windows looked over the city. The blinds were half-closed, turning the late afternoon into narrow bands of gray.

Marek sat behind a glass desk. His suit was charcoal, his cuffs unadorned. Across from him, the client placed a slim folder on the table and kept one hand resting on it.

“You said the footage was exclusive,” the client said.

“It is.”

“Not syndicated?”

“Not yet.”

The client opened the folder. Inside was a single photograph, face down.

Marek didn’t look at it. “The material is delivered in three stages. Preview, verification copy, final master.”

“Verification copy.”

“A controlled segment. Enough to establish authenticity. Not enough to circulate.”

“And the master?”

“Encrypted. Watermarked to your account. If it appears anywhere outside the agreed channel, the watermark identifies the source.”

The client closed the folder. “You’ve had leaks.”

“Everyone has had leaks.”

“I’m not everyone.”

“That remains to be demonstrated.”

For the first time, the client smiled. “You charge a great deal for demonstration.”

“I charge for certainty.”

Marek slid a printed sheet across the desk. It contained three numbers and a date.

The client studied it. “This is higher than the estimate.”

“The estimate was for a standard production.”

“And this?”

“Restricted distribution. Additional screening. Separate storage. Removal of all incidental material.”

“Incidental material?”

“Anything that identifies location, personnel, equipment, or sequence.”

“You’re saying the final cut is clean.”

“I’m saying the final cut contains only what you are paying for.”

The client tapped the paper once. “I want the original files.”

“No.”

“I’m paying for the rights.”

“You’re paying for access.”

“That distinction wasn’t in our correspondence.”

“It is now.”

Silence settled between them. Somewhere below, a siren moved through traffic and faded.

The client leaned back. “Suppose I want revisions.”

“Specify them before delivery.”

“Suppose I want something added afterward.”

“That becomes a new commission.”

“Suppose I want the entire package destroyed once I’ve reviewed it.”

“Then you pay for destruction.”

“Of the copies?”

“Of the copies, the records, and the people who handled them.”

The client looked at him carefully.

Marek’s expression did not change. “You asked for confidentiality.”

“I asked for discretion.”

“They are different products.”

The client turned the photograph over.

Marek watched the client’s eyes move across it, then return to the first line of the document.

“Delivery date?”

“Seventy-two hours after payment clears.”

“Too long.”

“It is the shortest reliable interval.”

“Can you guarantee the subject?”

“I can guarantee the production.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“It is the only guarantee available.”

The client closed the folder and placed it beside the printed sheet. “You make this sound like manufacturing.”

“It is manufacturing.”

“Of what?”

Marek reached for a pen and signed the bottom of the page.

“An item with a buyer.”

He pushed the contract across the desk.

The client read the final clause. “No refunds.”

“There are no refunds.”

“Even if the result is unsatisfactory?”

“Unsatisfactory is not a technical term.”

“And if the result is unusable?”

“That would be a failure of your specifications.”

The client considered him for several seconds, then uncapped a fountain pen.

Marek stood and walked to the window. Below, pedestrians crossed at the light, each moving according to signals they trusted.

Behind him, paper turned. Ink touched the page.

“Payment instructions,” the client said.

“Attached.”

“And the first preview?”

“Tomorrow evening.”

“Where?”

“You’ll receive a location.”

“Will you be there?”

“No.”

“Who will?”

“Someone who doesn’t need to know your name.”

The client rose, leaving the signed contract on the desk.

Marek gathered the pages, checked the signature, and placed them in a drawer.

“Pleasure doing business,” the client said.

Marek looked toward the window.

“Business is not improved by pleasure,” he said. “It is improved by completion.”

The snow had buried the wreckage up to its windows, turning the plane into a dark, frozen box. Inside, the survivors sat shoulder to shoulder beneath coats that no longer kept them warm. No one spoke about the body at the back.

They had spoken around it for two days.

He was dead before the storm closed in. Everyone knew that. There had been no chance of bringing him back, no breath to count, no pulse beneath the blue skin. Still, the living had treated him like a sleeping man. They had left his shoes on. They had covered his face. They had apologized whenever they moved his arm.

On the third morning, Mara found herself staring at the packet of matches in her lap.

“Don’t,” someone whispered.

She hadn’t said anything.

“I know what you’re thinking.”

Outside, the wind dragged itself across the fuselage with a long metallic moan. Inside, the cold had become something intimate, a presence tucked beneath her ribs. Her hands shook constantly now. Her thoughts arrived slowly, detached from one another. She remembered her daughter’s birthday, then the color of the emergency blanket, then the fact that she had not urinated since yesterday. Each fact floated by without meaning.

The pilot was the one who finally spoke.

“We don’t have to make it mean anything.”

Mara looked at him.

“It means he’s dead,” he said. “It means we’re not. That’s all.”

But it did mean something. It meant crossing a line that had existed before language—older than family, older than prayer. It meant taking the body they had guarded from hunger and admitting that hunger had become the stronger law.

They made rules because rules were easier than courage. No one would eat alone. No one would take more than anyone else. They would say his name first.

When they uncovered him, the cabin seemed to shrink. Mara focused on his face, on the familiar notch in his eyebrow, on the absurd detail of a thread loose at his collar. She waited for revulsion to save her. It didn’t. Revulsion had burned away sometime during the second night.

The pilot said his name.

One by one, they repeated it.

Mara held the portion in both hands. It was wrapped in cloth so she wouldn’t have to see it clearly. That mercy lasted until she brought it to her mouth.

Her body recoiled. Her throat closed. For one instant she was not in the wreckage but in her mother’s kitchen, being told that some things were unthinkable. The word rose inside her—*no*—clean and absolute.

Then the cold tightened around her lungs.

She thought of the storm outside. Of the mountain keeping its silence. Of the others watching her, not with accusation but with the terrible hope that she would prove this was possible.

Mara shut her eyes.

The first bite was not an act of appetite. It was an act of surrender—not to savagery, but to the fact that the world had narrowed to breath, warmth, and another hour alive.

She chewed once.

Nothing happened. No lightning. No punishment. The dead man did not return to her eyes as a monster or a sacrifice. He remained himself: someone who had been afraid, someone who had laughed too loudly, someone whose name they had spoken aloud before taking what his death could still give.

Mara swallowed.

Across from her, the youngest survivor began to cry. The pilot lowered his head. And for a while, the only sound inside the crushed plane was the quiet, methodical work of the living trying not to become ghosts.

The house stood at the end of Briar Lane, where the road narrowed into weeds and the streetlamps stopped trying.

People in town called Elias Vane a collector.

He collected clocks that had stopped at significant moments, porcelain birds with chipped beaks, wedding photographs found in junk shops. But his finest collection occupied the locked room beneath the house.

There were nine figures inside.

They stood beneath glass domes or behind velvet ropes, arranged as carefully as museum exhibits. Each wore the clothes they had disappeared in. Each held a familiar object: a brass key, a red scarf, a silver lighter. Elias had made small plaques for them, though he never wrote their names.

**THE TRAVELER.**  
**THE SINGER.**  
**THE MAN WHO LIED.**

He told himself the labels were merciful. Names belonged to the living.

On a rainy Thursday in November, Elias brought down his newest acquisition.

She had been a botanist, he decided, because of the green stains beneath her fingernails and the pressed leaves in her coat pocket. He placed her on the worktable beneath the white electric lamp and stood with his hands folded behind his back.

“Everyone deserves to be remembered accurately,” he said.

The room smelled of dust, polish, and the faint medicinal sharpness of things kept too long in sealed containers. On the walls hung diagrams from old books, faded photographs of natural-history museums, and handwritten notes in Elias’s narrow script.

He worked slowly.

He removed the signs of the journey first: rainwater from her hair, mud from her shoes, the torn thread at her sleeve. He dressed her in a dark green coat he had bought years ago, one that made her look as though she belonged among the trees.

Then he began the part he called *the correction*.

It was not about making a body lifelike. Elias had learned that the dead were never lifelike. They were too still, too honest. His task was to make stillness seem intentional—to suggest that the person might speak if the room were quiet enough.

He positioned her hands around a small glass vial. He tilted her head toward the door. He adjusted the angle of her chin again and again until the expression on her face became something almost peaceful.

Almost.

For the inner structure, he used materials from the cabinet marked **MISCELLANEOUS**. He never thought of what had once been inside the people. Thinking too closely about that made the work sentimental, and sentiment ruined precision. What mattered was silhouette, balance, the impression of presence.

At midnight, he stepped back.

The woman stood beneath the lamp in her green coat, one hand resting against the glass vial, her eyes fixed on the locked door.

Elias felt the familiar satisfaction settle over him.

Not pride. Pride was vulgar.

Completion.

He carried her upstairs just before dawn and installed her in the eastern alcove, between the Traveler and the Singer. He mounted a new brass plaque beneath the glass:

**THE GARDENER.**

For several minutes, he admired the arrangement.

Then the house made a sound.

A soft tapping came from beneath the dome.

Elias froze.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

He turned toward the new exhibit.

The Gardener’s hand had moved.

Only slightly. The fingers were now curled around the vial.

Elias approached the glass. His reflection hovered over the woman’s face, making it difficult to tell where he ended and she began.

Tap.

This time, the sound came from inside the vial.

He lifted it from her hand and held it to the light. At first he saw only cloudy liquid. Then something dark drifted up from the bottom—thin as a root, twisting slowly in the suspension.

Behind him, the other exhibits began to tap against their glass.

One by one.

A rhythm passed through the room, delicate and patient.

Elias looked at the plaques.

The names he had refused to write seemed to appear beneath the labels, emerging from the brass as if pressed upward from underneath.

**MARA BELL.**  
**THOMAS REED.**  
**JONAH PRICE.**

The figures turned their heads toward him.

Not far. Not dramatically.

Just enough.

Elias backed toward the door, but the lock would not open. He pulled at it until his fingernails split. The tapping grew louder, surrounding him now, filling the room like rain.

On the worktable below, the instruments of his craft began to tremble.

The Gardener lifted her face.

For the first time, Elias saw her expression clearly.

It was not peaceful.

It was patient.

And from somewhere inside the walls, beneath the floorboards and behind the plaster, came the sound of a tenth person knocking to be let in.

The room smelled wrong.

Not merely rotten—though rot was there, thick and sweet beneath the sting of bleach. It was the smell of a butcher’s drain left warm in the sun, of metal gone sour, of something organic sealed in plastic and forgotten.

Evan sat strapped to a steel chair, wrists pinned beneath leather cuffs. A clear tube ran from the ceiling to a glass bowl on the table in front of him. Inside it, something pale floated in cloudy pink fluid.

A monitor flickered to life.

“YOU HAVE SIX MINUTES.”

The voice was distorted, almost mechanical.

“Consume the contents of the bowl. If you fail, the mechanism beneath your chair will activate.”

Evan stared at the bowl.

At first he thought the pale mass was a heart. Then it twitched.

A cluster of black beetles crawled over it, disappearing into folds of slick tissue. Their legs clicked against the glass. One surfaced from a red slit and dragged itself across the organ, leaving a faint trail in the fluid.

Evan’s stomach contracted.

“No,” he whispered.

A gear turned beneath him.

The chair’s metal frame gave a sharp, warning jerk.

He gagged before he even touched it. Saliva flooded his mouth, hot and sudden. He tried to swallow, but his throat had already closed around the reflex. His stomach lurched hard enough to pull him forward against the restraints.

The monitor counted down.

**05:21**

“Please,” Evan said, though there was no one to hear him. “Please, I can’t—”

The bowl was fitted with a narrow funnel. He had to lift it to his mouth and pour.

His fingers shook so badly that the glass knocked against his teeth.

The smell hit him fully.

Warm iron. Sour fat. Damp soil. A rancid sweetness that coated the back of his throat without him even swallowing. His eyes watered. He turned his head, but the restraints forced his face back toward the bowl.

One of the beetles crawled over the rim.

Evan made a strangled noise.

The mechanism beneath the chair clicked again.

He seized the bowl.

The first mouthful slid onto his tongue.

It was cold, then warm. Soft in the center, rubbery at the edges. The texture collapsed between his teeth with a wet, fibrous give. A beetle struck the roof of his mouth and skittered toward his throat.

He gagged violently.

His jaw spasmed. He tried to spit, but the funnel was still pressed to his lips, and the bowl’s contents sloshed forward. A thread of cloudy fluid ran down his chin. He choked on it, coughing so hard his vision blurred.

The thing in his mouth moved.

That was what broke him.

He heaved against the straps, making the chair screech across the floor. His stomach convulsed, but the first mouthful clung stubbornly to his tongue and teeth. He clamped both hands over his mouth, trapping the foul mass inside.

The monitor ticked down.

**04:38**

His lungs burned. His throat stretched around a swallow he did not want to make.

Evan shut his eyes.

He thought of nothing but numbers.

One.

He forced his throat to work.

Two.

The tissue slid down like a lump of wet cloth.

Three.

The beetle followed.

He gagged again, but this time there was nothing to bring up except strings of saliva. His body kept trying anyway, his abdomen jerking beneath his shirt, his eyes streaming. A thin, bubbling belch escaped him, carrying the taste back up—copper, grease, decay.

He nearly vomited.

The chair groaned.

“No,” he rasped. “No, no, no—”

He lifted the bowl again.

More of the organ slumped toward the funnel. A beetle clung to the underside, its legs paddling against the glass. Evan watched it approach his mouth and felt his entire body recoil before he could stop it.

He poured.

The second mouthful struck his tongue like cold jelly. He bit down reflexively. Something popped between his molars.

His gag reflex fired so hard that his vision flashed white.

He swallowed anyway.

Then again.

And again.

By the time the bowl was empty, Evan’s face was slick with tears, saliva, and pink liquid. He hung limply in the chair, trembling, his throat working in useless aftershocks. Every breath carried the taste of the room back into him.

The monitor went black.

A lock released beneath the chair.

For several seconds, Evan could do nothing but cough.

Then the speaker crackled.

“CONSUMPTION VERIFIED.”

The door opened.

Beyond it waited another dark corridor.

Evan looked at the empty bowl. One final beetle crawled along the glass, searching for a way out.

He stumbled from the chair, gagging at the sight, and ran.

The temple had been carved into the black heart of the mountain, where no sunlight reached and the air smelled of wet stone, old incense, and iron.

At its center stood the altar: a slab of basalt darkened by generations of offerings. The victim lay bound upon it, breath coming in ragged bursts, eyes fixed on the priest. Around them, hooded worshipers murmured behind bone-white masks, their voices rising and falling like wind through a crypt.

The priest did not look at the crowd. He did not look at the trembling figure beneath him.

He lifted the sacrificial knife with both hands.

Its blade was narrow and polished, reflecting the guttering torchlight in a cold line. The victim pleaded once. The priest’s face remained empty—not cruel, not angry, not even solemn. His expression had the blank patience of a man performing a task he had repeated too many times to remember beginning.

He pressed the knife into the flesh below the ribs.

The first cut opened slowly. Blood welled, bright against the gray skin, then spilled down the sides of the altar in thin streams. The victim jerked against the bindings, heels striking stone. The priest adjusted his grip with practical care, as though correcting the angle of a tool.

When the blade sank deeper, the body convulsed. A wet choking sound escaped the victim’s throat. The priest watched the wound, not the face, measuring the sacrifice by its bleeding. He made another incision, precise and deliberate, widening the opening until the altar ran red.

The chanting grew louder.

Still, the priest’s expression did not change. He reached into the wound and withdrew the steaming heart, holding it above the altar while blood ran over his fingers. The organ shuddered once in his palm.

Only then did he raise his eyes to the idol looming behind him—a faceless god carved from obsidian.

“Received,” he said.

His voice held no triumph. No disgust. No prayer.

He placed the heart in the stone bowl at the idol’s feet, wiped the blade clean on the victim’s robe, and turned toward the next kneeling figure as the body on the altar continued to twitch.

The light had begun to thin at the edges.

It drained from the alley in slow, quiet layers—the gold above the rooftops fading first, then the gray of the brick, then the dark shape of my own hand pressed against my side. I could still see it, but only because it moved. My fingers trembled. The blood between them shone almost black.

I tried to sit up.

The wall behind me was cold enough to burn. My shoulder slipped against the damp brick, and the movement sent a bright flare through my ribs. For a moment, the alley sharpened around me: the overturned crate, the narrow strip of sky, the knife lying several feet away with its blade turned toward the last of the light.

Then everything softened again.

Thud.

My heartbeat sounded too loud.

Thud.

It filled my skull, each beat separated from the next by a long, hollow pause.

I counted them without meaning to. Ten. Eleven. Twelve.

The cold was spreading upward from my legs. At first it had been the ordinary cold of evening, seeping through my clothes. Now it had weight. It wrapped around my knees and climbed into my stomach, my chest, my hands. I could no longer feel the fingers pressed to the wound. They belonged to someone else—someone standing nearby, perhaps, watching me make a poor attempt at holding myself together.

I remembered the knife fight in fragments.

A flash of steel.

His breath, ragged and close.

My own hand closing around his wrist.

The impact of the blade.

After that, the memory broke apart. There had been shouting somewhere beyond the alley. A door slamming. Footsteps that came near and then vanished.

No one was coming now.

I lifted my face toward the sky. The strip between the buildings had turned the color of deep water. One star appeared, faint and uncertain. I wondered if it had been there all along, hidden by the brightness.

Thud.

The pause stretched longer.

I held my breath, waiting for the next beat.

There.

Thud.

A wave of dizziness moved through me. I shut my eyes, but darkness did not make things simpler. Behind my eyelids, pale shapes drifted and dissolved. My mother’s kitchen. A summer field. The crooked smile of someone whose name I could no longer reach.

The cold had found my chest now. Each breath came shallow, scraping at the back of my throat. I wanted to pull my coat tighter, but my arms had become heavy. I could barely keep one hand against my side.

The blood had warmed me at first.

Now it was cooling beneath my palm.

Thud.

I listened to it with the fascination of a child listening through a wall. It was the only proof I had left that I was still here. The alley, the bricks, the knife, the fading sky—all of them seemed farther away than that sound.

Thud.

My heartbeat faltered.

I opened my eyes.

The star was gone. Or perhaps the darkness had simply swallowed it. The rooftops had vanished, and the walls were no more than tall shadows leaning inward. I thought I heard footsteps again, soft and hurried, but they might have been inside my head.

I tried to call out.

Nothing came.

The cold reached my throat.

Thud.

A pause.

Thud.

The light narrowed to a thin silver line above me.

I fixed my eyes on it and listened.

Thud.

The line became a point.

Thud.

Then, for a long moment, there was only the cold—

and the silence waiting after it.

results.model_response:
Detective Mara Venn found the note beneath the rabbit’s empty hutch.

It was folded twice, carefully—more carefully than the rest of the room had been left. The kitchen chair lay on its side. A glass had shattered against the wall. Muddy footprints crossed the linoleum and stopped at the back door.

But the note was clean.

Mara pulled on her gloves and opened it.

The paper had been torn from a school notebook. Blue lines ran through the message, and every letter was pressed so hard into the page that the pencil had nearly ripped through.

> **Dear Detective,**  
>   
> I had to hurt Button because he wouldn’t tell me where she went.  
>   
> I asked him nicely. I gave him three chances. He just looked at me with those shiny black eyes, like he knew and was keeping it secret.  
>   
> Mommy says animals don’t understand words, but Button understood mine. I could tell.  
>   
> I didn’t want to do it. I only wanted him to be honest.  
>   
> He made me do it because he stayed quiet.  
>   
> Please don’t be angry with me. I’m not bad. Bad people do things for fun.  
>   
> I did it because I had to.  
>   
> **P.S.** If you find Mommy before I do, don’t let her talk to Button. He lies when she’s around.

Mara read it twice.

The house was silent except for the slow ticking of the clock above the sink.

On the floor beside the hutch sat a child’s red rain boot, still wet from the yard. The other boot was missing. A trail of small footprints led away from the back door and vanished into the tall grass beyond the fence.

Mara folded the note along its old creases.

Then, from somewhere upstairs, a child’s voice called softly:

“Detective?”

Mara looked toward the ceiling.

“Did he tell you where she went?”

The mercenary kicked the door inward and raised the flamethrower.

The room erupted in orange light.

Heat struck first—a crushing wave that dried the air in his throat and made the visor of his mask shimmer. He squeezed the trigger, and the weapon answered with a deep, pressurized roar. Fire rolled across the room in a broad, liquid sheet, swallowing barricades, desks, and the figures crouched behind them.

The smell came a heartbeat later: fuel, scorched plastic, smoke, and the sickening odor of flesh burning beneath cloth and armor. It clung to the back of his throat despite the filter.

The enemies shouted. One fired blindly into the flames. Another staggered toward the far exit, hands beating at fire that would not go out. Their screams rose above the roar of the weapon—sharp at first, then ragged and hoarse, until smoke and heat swallowed the sound.

The mercenary swept the nozzle from left to right. Fire crawled over the walls and ceiling, turning posters black and bursting the light fixtures. Shadows thrashed behind the flames. A rifle clattered across the floor. Someone pounded once against the sealed emergency door, then stopped.

He held the stream a moment longer, watching the room’s resistance collapse into sparks and smoke.

When he released the trigger, the sudden silence seemed louder than the flamethrower had been. Embers drifted through the dark. The air remained brutally hot, carrying the bitter smell of ash and burned insulation.

He stepped over the threshold, boots crunching across broken glass, and checked the corners.

“Room clear,” he said, though no one answered.
