Mara noticed the first patch of shedding skin beneath her left wrist.

At first, it looked like sunburn. Then the skin began to loosen in translucent strips, peeling away whenever she moved. Beneath it was something darker and tougher, gray as wet stone, threaded with faint blue veins. She tried to bandage it, but the gauze stuck and came away carrying more of herself with it.

The changes spread.

Her fingers lengthened by degrees, the joints swelling before snapping back into new positions. At night, she woke to the sound of her own bones grinding together. Her spine bowed, vertebra by vertebra, forcing her shoulders forward. Ribs pressed outward beneath her skin, cracking one after another as her chest widened. Each break brought a brief, blinding agony—followed by the awful relief of a body settling into a shape it had been waiting to assume.

She stopped screaming after the third night.

What frightened her most was not the pain, but how quickly she adapted to it. She learned which movements would make a knee bend backward, which fingers could curl around a door handle, how to breathe through a throat that was narrowing and lengthening at once. Her reflection became less recognizable: eyes filmed with gold, teeth crowded into sharp new rows, a jaw that seemed to hang too heavily from her skull.

Her conscience changed more quietly.

At first, she still felt guilty when she frightened people. Then she began to resent them for being frightened. Their faces seemed soft and foolish, their voices irritatingly high. Hunger became an argument that defeated every other argument. She told herself that the instincts were not hers, that the thing growing inside her was responsible—but the distinction grew harder to maintain.

One evening, her brother found her crouched in the kitchen, surrounded by the splintered remains of the furniture.

“Mara,” he whispered.

She turned toward him. A final sheet of human skin slid from her cheek and fell soundlessly to the floor.

For one heartbeat, she remembered loving him.

Then the memory became an obstacle: an old chain around the throat of something stronger.

Her new mouth opened, and what came out was not her name.

The first handful of dirt struck the coffin lid with a soft, heavy thump.

Mara flinched so hard her shoulders hit the wood behind her. For one wild second, she imagined the lid flexing beneath the weight. It didn’t. It only answered with another thump, then another, each one dull and final.

Above her, someone was shoveling.

She pressed both palms against the lid. The wood was cold and close enough that her elbows scraped the coffin walls. There was no room to sit up, no room to turn her head without bumping her temple. Her knees were bent sharply, her boots wedged against the far end. Every breath brought her ribs against the lining.

“Stop!” she shouted.

The word came back to her in a tiny, muffled echo.

Dirt rattled across the lid.

Thump.

A pause.

Thump-thump.

The sounds traveled through the wood and into her bones. Loose soil whispered down the sides of the coffin. It made a dry, granular hiss, like rain against a window—only there was no window, no sky, no distance. Just six walls and the darkness pressing in from every side.

Mara pounded on the lid.

“Stop! I’m here!”

Her knuckles struck hard enough to hurt. The impact bounced back into her hands. She hit it again, faster, until pain flared through her fingers.

The dirt kept falling.

Thump.

The coffin seemed to shrink around her.

She tried to draw a deep breath and couldn’t. Air entered her lungs in a thin, hot sip. She tried again. The same. Her own breath returned against her face, warmer each time, carrying the damp smell of panic. The inside of the coffin had already begun to smell of pine, earth, and the sour salt of her skin.

She forced herself to stop shouting.

Listen.

Maybe the shoveling had stopped. Maybe—

Thump.

The sound was directly overhead now. Closer. Heavier.

A faint tremor passed through the lid. Dirt slid toward the edges, ticking against the wood in tiny streams. Mara pictured it piling above her: a dark, crushing blanket growing inch by inch. The image was worse than the darkness. She could see it even with her eyes squeezed shut.

She clawed at the lining near her shoulder, searching for some impossible gap. Her fingernails caught in the fabric. She tore it, then tore deeper, finding only padding beneath. The coffin walls pressed against her arms. There was nowhere to put her hands. Nowhere to move the frantic energy trapped inside her body.

Her heart hammered so violently it seemed to fill the whole coffin.

Thump-thump-thump.

The rhythm quickened.

Or perhaps it was only her pulse.

Mara turned her face toward the narrow space near her mouth. The air there felt marginally cooler. She opened her lips and took a careful breath, but the breath snagged halfway in. Her chest fluttered. She swallowed against the tightening in her throat.

Don’t waste it, she told herself.

The dirt struck again, louder now, the lid answering with a deep wooden boom.

She imagined the person above: boots planted beside the grave, arms lifting, shovel biting into the earth. Perhaps they were taking their time. Perhaps they could hear her. Perhaps each shovelful was deliberate.

Another impact.

Dust sifted down through a seam near her ear. It touched her cheek. She jerked away, though there was nowhere to go.

The darkness became physical. It had weight. It pressed against her eyelids, her teeth, the soft spaces beneath her ribs. She felt buried not only beneath the ground but inside it, absorbed by it, sealed away.

She screamed again.

The coffin swallowed the sound.

For a moment, there was silence.

Mara held her breath, listening.

Nothing.

Then, faintly, the scrape of a shovel.

A pause.

The first clump landed with a crushing thud.

She kicked the lid. Once. Twice. The coffin gave a hollow groan.

More dirt fell.

Thump.

Thump.

Thump.

The air grew hotter. Thinner. Each breath became an argument her body was losing. She pressed her mouth to the wood and tried to pull in whatever air remained, but the lid smelled of varnish and soil. Her lungs worked faster, stealing from the shrinking pocket around her face.

Above, the shovel kept moving.

Below, Mara curled as tightly as the coffin allowed and listened to the earth closing over her, one heavy handful at a time.

The operating hall had once been a train station. The old departure boards still hung above the rows of surgical tables, their letters clicking uselessly between destinations that no longer existed. Beneath them, citizens lay strapped beneath white lamps while the state’s engineers converted them into instruments.

No one was given anesthesia. The government called pain “proof of adaptation.”

A woman screamed as metal braces were fastened along her spine. The sound echoed through the vaulted ceiling, then dissolved beneath the hiss of drills and the steady, mechanical voice of a technician reciting her new designation. Her hands had been replaced with articulated tools, each finger jointed in polished steel. When she looked down, she saw wires disappearing beneath her skin like black roots.

Across the room, a boy no older than sixteen was fitted with glass lenses over his eyes. He begged for his mother, but the lenses brightened, recording the movement of the surgeon’s hands. A green light blinked at his temple.

“Subject responsive,” someone said.

That was all he became: responsive.

The machines did not merely cut into flesh. They erased the small, private things that made a person recognizable—the tremor in a hand, the warmth of a touch, the face someone loved. Names were removed from the charts and replaced with numbers. Voices were filtered until they sounded alike. Memories were not considered necessary equipment.

When the tables finally rose, the altered figures stood unsteadily, connected to the walls by cables. ### The Geometry of Silence

By the time I arrived, the rain had washed the street clean.

That was the first thing I noticed: not the body, not the overturned chair, not the yellow tape trembling between the elms, but the immaculate pavement shining beneath the police lamps. Every stone reflected a broken piece of the night. Blue. Gold. White. Blue again.

I had been a forensic investigator for eleven years, long enough to know that a crime scene was never beautiful.

Beauty implied intention. Harmony. A promise that the eye could trust what it saw.

A crime scene offered none of those things.

And yet, sometimes, it arranged itself with such terrible precision that I had to resist the urge to call it beautiful.

The house stood at the end of a narrow lane, a former conservatory owned by a woman named Celia Vale. She had been a pianist, though the newspapers would later call her an eccentric and, once the facts became dull, a recluse. The house had belonged to her father, then to her, and for thirty years she had filled it with glass, music, and plants that grew wild beneath the vaulted roof.

Inside, the air was warm and wet.

The conservatory opened around me like the interior of a lantern. Moonlight filtered through the panes, dividing the tiled floor into pale rectangles. Ferns crowded the corners. White orchids hung from black iron hooks. Condensation blurred the glass until the garden beyond appeared submerged.

Celia Vale lay beside the piano.

She had been dressed in a dark green evening gown, though there was no evidence she had planned to go anywhere. Her silver hair had been pinned at the nape of her neck. One hand rested on the floor, fingers curved as if she had been about to touch a key. The other lay across her stomach.

There was blood, but not much.

A narrow, dark stain ran from her temple to the collar of her dress. It had dried in a thin line, almost delicate. Beneath her, the pale tiles had caught the spill in a fan-shaped pattern, each branch narrowing as it traveled away from her.

The piano stood open.

No music sheet had been left on the stand. Instead, a single white camellia lay across the keys.

I remember thinking: *It is composed.*

The thought disgusted me.

I knelt several feet away and began the work of dismantling the image.

Photographs first. Wide angles, then closer views. The room before anyone touched it. The body from every side. The piano, the flower, the footprints in the moisture near the door. I recorded the temperature. I marked the positions of the furniture. I listened while the detectives spoke in low voices behind me.

But the scene resisted being reduced to facts.

The camellia was not fresh. Its petals had begun to brown at the edges. There was soil on the stem, suggesting it had been cut from one of the garden beds. The keys beneath it were spotless except for a single smear of red near middle C.

The blood trail from Celia’s temple was too narrow for the injury we had initially assumed. The wound was small, but the force behind it had been significant. She had not fallen where she had been struck. She had been moved.

That detail should have broken the spell.

Instead, it deepened it.

Someone had lifted her and placed her beside the piano with care. Someone had arranged her hand. Someone had taken the time to find a flower, carry it through the damp conservatory, and lay it on the keys.

The murderer had not merely killed her.

They had edited her.

I began to see arrangements everywhere.

At the next scene, a man had been found in his apartment beneath a window. The blinds cast horizontal shadows across the room, and his blood had dried in parallel streaks on the hardwood. I spent twenty minutes photographing the patterns before realizing I was waiting for the sunlight to shift.

After that came a woman in a hotel room, surrounded by discarded dresses. The clothes formed concentric circles around her body, satin and wool and black lace, as if she were the center of some private orbit. I noticed the colors before I noticed the bruising.

A child’s bedroom contained no body at all, only an empty bed, a broken night-light, and a row of small muddy footprints leading to the wall. The detectives called it a disappearance. I called it an installation in my notes, then crossed the word out so violently that the paper tore.

I started keeping photographs.

Not official copies. Mine.

I printed them at home and stored them in envelopes labeled by date. I told myself I was studying patterns—how objects drew the eye, how light transformed a room, how violence disturbed the ordinary geometry of domestic life.

Soon I was rearranging my apartment.

I moved the chairs so they faced the windows. I placed bowls of fruit beneath lamps. I bought white flowers and let them decay in water. My walls filled with images of rooms that had been invaded by death.

When my sister visited, she stood among the photographs and said nothing for a long time.

“You should take these down,” she said.

“They help me understand.”

“No,” she said. “They help you look.”

I stopped inviting her over.

The case of Celia Vale remained unsolved for eight months.

The police believed the killer was someone she knew. There had been no forced entry, and nothing valuable had been taken. Her neighbors reported no argument, no raised voices, no unfamiliar car. The most likely explanation was that she had opened the door willingly.

But I could not forget the room.

In my mind, the conservatory became more exact with every recollection. I remembered the droplets trembling on the orchids. The thin crescent of dust beneath the piano bench. The dark red line beside the green silk. I began to dream of the camellia opening and closing like a mouth.

Then, one afternoon, I found the missing detail.

It was buried in an old photograph taken before the body had been removed. I was reviewing the case file for no particular reason when I saw something in the reflection of the piano’s polished side.

A second flower.

Not on the keys. Reflected in the black lacquer, near the far edge of the room.

I enlarged the image until the pixels broke apart. There it was: another white shape beneath the vines, partially hidden by the piano bench.

The house had been sealed for months, but the conservatory was still warm and green. Police tape had faded to a dull yellow. Dust softened the piano’s contours. The garden had grown over the paths.

I searched beneath the bench and found nothing.

Then I noticed the floor.

One tile was slightly darker than the others. I scraped away the dirt with my glove and found a narrow brass key embedded in the grout.

It opened a drawer in Celia’s writing desk.

Inside was a notebook.

The pages contained no names, no confession, no explanation. Only descriptions of rooms.

Celia had written about the conservatory in astonishing detail: the changing color of the morning light, the sound of rain against the roof, the way the orchids bent toward the glass. But near the end, the entries became stranger.

*The room is most honest after something has been broken.*

*Every object reveals its proper shape when placed beside loss.*

*I wonder whether terror can be made perfect.*

The final page held a drawing of the piano.

On the keys, she had sketched a white camellia.

The murderer was arrested three weeks later. He had been Celia’s former student, a man who believed she had stolen his music and ruined his career. He confessed to the killing, to moving the body, to placing the flower.

But he denied writing the notebook.

That was the part no one could explain.

The final report called the scene “deliberately staged.” It described the body, the weapon, the blood, the flower. It used the language of evidence, which is the language I had once trusted to keep me separate from what I saw.

I submitted my photographs.

I destroyed the ones I had kept at home.

All but one.

It was a wide shot of the conservatory before the investigators entered. Rain shone on the glass. The piano waited in the corner. Celia lay beside it, small and still, surrounded by green leaves and fractured moonlight.

I keep the photograph facedown in a drawer.

Sometimes I take it out.

Not because it is beautiful.

Because I am afraid that it is.

The rope creaked over the mesquite branch.

Dust moved low across the road, whispering around the boots of the men who had gathered to watch. Beyond them, the town sat silent beneath the white blaze of noon—false-front buildings, shuttered windows, a church steeple leaning into the sky.

Elias Vane stood on the wagon bed with his hands tied behind him. The noose rested against his throat, rough hemp dark with sweat. He looked over the crowd once, searching faces, finding none that would meet his eyes.

The sheriff climbed down from the wagon.

For a moment, nothing moved but the flies.

Then he slapped the horse’s flank.

The animal lurched forward. The wagon rolled out from beneath Elias, and the rope snapped taut with a hard jerk. His body dropped, boots kicking clear of the ground.

There was a sharp, ugly crack from his neck—not loud, but unmistakable, like a green branch broken across a knee.

A murmur passed through the crowd and died just as quickly.

Elias’s hat fell into the dust. His body swung slowly beneath the branch, turning with the wind. His boots jerked once, then again, scraping at empty air. His fingers clenched against the rope binding them, and a shudder ran through his shoulders. For several long seconds, his legs twitched in uneven spasms, leather soles flashing beneath him.

The mesquite creaked.

No one spoke.

At last, the motion dwindled to a faint sway. The rope groaned with each turn, and the dead man’s coat lifted and settled in the hot wind.

The sheriff stared up at him, jaw tight.

“Let that be a lesson,” he said.

But the only answer was the dry rattle of leaves and the distant cry of a hawk.

The alley lay between two shuttered buildings, narrow as a throat and black beneath the broken fire escape. Rainwater glimmered in the gutters, carrying scraps of paper toward the street.

The vampire heard the victim before he saw him: uneven footsteps, the rasp of breath, the quickened rhythm of a heart trying to outrun the night.

Hunger moved through him like a second pulse.

He stepped from the shadows.

The victim turned, mouth opening to shout, but the vampire crossed the distance in an instant. One hand clamped over the man’s mouth; the other caught his shoulder and drove him against the brick. The impact knocked the air from him.

For a moment, the vampire only listened.

The heartbeat hammered beneath the skin. Warm blood rushed through the throat, thick with fear. Hunger sharpened everything—the rain ticking against metal, the scent of wet stone, the living heat trembling under his grasp. His fangs ached as they lengthened.

Then he bent his head.

The puncture was quick: two small wounds beneath the jaw, followed by a startled cry muffled against his palm. Blood welled around the bites, dark in the alley’s weak light. The vampire drank.

The victim struggled at first, fists striking uselessly against the vampire’s chest. His heartbeat raced faster, then began to falter. Strength drained from his limbs in slow increments. His knees buckled, and the hand gripping the vampire’s sleeve slipped lower, fingers twitching as though searching for something solid to hold.

Still, the hunger demanded more.

The vampire drank until the man’s breath became shallow and thin, until the frantic pulse beneath his lips weakened to a flutter. The victim’s face had gone pale, his eyes unfocused beneath half-lowered lids. His resistance faded into a faint shudder.

At last, the vampire pulled away.

Blood marked his mouth. He stared down at the body slumped against the wall, listening to the fragile heartbeat that remained. The hunger had quieted, but not vanished. It never vanished.

He released the victim, who slid slowly to the wet pavement, one hand pressed weakly to his throat.

Above them, the fire escape groaned in the wind. By the time headlights swept across the mouth of the alley, the vampire was gone—leaving only two small wounds, a smear of blood on the bricks, and the fading sound of a heartbeat in the dark.

Mara ran without knowing what she was running from.

The forest flashed around her in fragments—silver birch, black branches, the pale churn of moonlit fog. Behind her, nothing moved. No footfall. No breath. No snapping twig to mark the distance between herself and whatever had chosen her.

Then something struck her back.

It felt like a fist made of ice. The impact drove the air from her lungs and sent her sprawling across the wet leaves. For a moment she could only lie there, cheek pressed to the mud, tasting iron. Her fingers clawed uselessly at the ground.

When she tried to rise, pain opened beneath her ribs—sudden, deep, and precise. Not a stab, exactly. More like invisible fingers pushing into her flesh and slowly twisting. She screamed and heard the sound vanish among the trees.

There was no wound she could see. Only warmth spreading beneath her shirt. Her hand came away slick with blood.

The forest remained empty.

Mara staggered upright. Every breath scraped against the injury. Something brushed past her left arm, though the air was still. A line of fire sprang from her shoulder to her wrist, and her fingers went numb. She spun, striking at nothing. Her palm met only cold mist.

The room had once been a chapel.

Her friends knelt in a row on the stone floor.

Beside him, Elian stared straight ahead, pale and rigid, his hands bound behind his back. Sera was crying silently. She had always been the brave one. That was what made it worse.

The executioner stood behind them with a long-handled axe resting against his shoulder.

At the far end of the chapel, beneath the cracked wooden cross, sat the governor.

“Three prisoners,” he said. “One blade.”

Mara’s wrists were free, but guards stood on either side of her. Freedom had become another kind of restraint. They had dragged her here because she had been the one who knew them best—their habits, their loyalties, their weaknesses.

The governor leaned forward. “Choose one.”

Her lungs seemed to forget how to work.

“No.”

The governor nodded to the executioner.

The axe came down into the stone beside Jonas’s hand.

The impact split the floor. Jonas flinched despite himself. Sera made a strangled noise.

“Choose,” the governor repeated, “or I will choose for you. All three.”

Jonas: the first person who had ever called her fearless, even when she was shaking.

Elian: who had carried her half a mile through snow after the bridge collapsed.

Sera: who had held Mara’s face between both hands when her brother died and told her that surviving was not a betrayal.

There was no answer that did not become a murder.

“Because they trust you.”

The governor’s words entered her like a nail.

Jonas lifted his head. “Mara.”

She couldn’t look at him.

“Mara, listen to me.”

“Don’t.”

“Listen.” His voice was wet and ragged, but steady. “Pick me.”

Elian turned toward him. “No.”

Jonas gave a brittle laugh. “You always were slow.”

“Pick me,” Elian said.

Sera shook her head violently. “No. No, don’t—”

She imagined choosing Jonas. Elian’s face afterward.

She imagined choosing Elian. Sera’s empty stare.

She imagined choosing Sera. Jonas screaming.

The governor watched with mild interest, as if she were deciding which wine to serve.

“Mara,” Jonas said softly.

She finally met his eyes.

He was afraid. That was the terrible thing. Not noble, not calm, not transformed by courage. Afraid. His lower lip trembled. His eyes shone with the same animal panic she felt clawing through her own ribs.

But he was also asking her to make the pain end.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

Jonas closed his eyes.

Mara turned toward the governor.

“Elian.”

Silence.

Then Sera screamed.

Elian’s face did not change. Only his eyes moved, finding hers. For one heartbeat, she saw everything he might have said: You promised. I trusted you. It’s all right. It isn’t.

The executioner stepped behind him.

Mara began to shake so violently that her teeth struck together. “Wait,” she gasped. “Wait, please. I chose him. Just—give me a moment.”

The governor smiled. “You have had several years.”

Elian looked at Jonas, then at Sera.

“Don’t let them make it mean something,” he said.

The axe rose.

Mara screamed and surged forward. The guards caught her by the arms. Her shoulder tore with a hot, blinding pain. She kicked, clawed, begged. The chapel filled with the sound of her voice, but it could not reach the blade.

It fell.

The cut was not clean.

Steel struck bone with a heavy crack. Elian’s body jerked forward. Blood burst across the pale stones in a dark fan, spattering Jonas’s face and Sera’s dress. The axe lodged halfway through his neck. Then the executioner wrenched the weapon free.

Elian collapsed.

Sera vomited beside him. Jonas began to sob—not loudly, but with the broken, breathless rhythm of a child who had been hurt too many times.

Mara stopped struggling.

Mara looked down at Elian’s hand.

His fingers had curled around something before he died: a small brass key, the one they had stolen together on the night they first decided to resist.

She stared at it until the chapel blurred.

Then she picked it up.

And when the guards dragged her away, she carried the bloodied key in her fist so tightly that its teeth cut into her palm.

The first thing Daniel noticed was the smell.

It wasn’t the usual basement smell—damp concrete, rust, the sweet rot of leaves trapped against the foundation. This was sharper, medicinal, threaded with something metallic that caught in the back of his throat.

He stood at the bottom of his neighbor’s stairs, one hand gripping the banister, while rain tapped against the small windows above him.

“Mr. Vale?” he called.

No answer.

Daniel had only come over because Vale’s kitchen faucet had been running for nearly an hour. He’d seen the water spilling over the sink through the window and had knocked until the old man finally opened the door, pale and distracted.

“The shutoff’s in the basement,” Vale had said. “Would you mind?”

Then the doorbell rang. Vale went upstairs to answer it.

He never came back.

At first, Daniel assumed he had forgotten. Then he heard something fall behind the furnace room wall.

A dull, heavy thump.

“Mr. Vale?”

The basement was unfinished except for a narrow storage area at the far end. Daniel knew that much from seeing movers carry boxes through the house years ago. But now a tall metal cabinet stood in front of the storage door, its padlock hanging open.

The door behind it was ajar.

The smell came from there.

Daniel should have gone upstairs. He understood that later, when he tried to reconstruct the exact moment his life split into before and after. He should have left the house, called the police, waited in the rain.

Instead, he pulled the door wider.

A single bulb flickered overhead.

The room beyond was not a storage room. It was too clean for that. The concrete floor had been painted white, and every wall was lined with shelves. Glass jars stood in orderly rows beneath handwritten labels: dates, initials, locations.

Some held small objects—watches, rings, keys, hair ribbons, photographs folded at the corners. Others contained things Daniel couldn’t identify at first glance. Teeth, perhaps. Pieces of bone. A child’s red mitten stiffened with brown stains.

On the center wall hung a display of photographs.

Not crime-scene photographs. Portraits.

Men and women smiling at restaurants, standing beside cars, posing with family members. Ordinary moments stolen from ordinary lives. Each face had been circled in black marker. Beneath every photograph was a date.

Daniel took one step inside.

The air was colder than it should have been.

At the back of the room stood a long workbench covered with instruments: knives of different sizes, pliers, a surgical saw, coils of wire, bottles of clear liquid. Everything had been scrubbed spotless except for a dark smear near the edge of the table.

Beside it sat a row of shallow wooden boxes.

The lids were open.

Inside each box was a piece of someone’s life arranged with careful, terrible precision: a wedding band wrapped in cloth, a lock of hair tied with blue thread, a set of dentures, a bloodstained shoe. One box held a necklace Daniel recognized. He had seen it in the newspaper three months earlier, in a photograph of a woman who had disappeared while walking home from work.

His mouth went dry.

There were dozens of boxes.

Maybe more than a hundred.

At the center of the back wall, beneath a bright lamp, was the largest display. A mannequin stood there in a gray coat. Its face was covered by a human mask—pale, waxy, and unmistakably shaped like a man’s features. The skin had been stitched at the edges, the thread dark against the cheeks.

Daniel stared at it, unable to breathe.

Around the mannequin’s neck hung a laminated card.

THE NEIGHBOR, it read.

Underneath was a photograph.

Daniel.

Taken from across the street. Taken through his bedroom window, judging by the angle.

The photograph showed him sleeping.

A soft click came from behind him.

Daniel turned.

Mr. Vale stood in the doorway.

He had changed out of his house clothes. He wore a dark jacket and gloves. Rainwater gleamed on his shoulders, though Daniel hadn’t heard the front door open.

For a moment neither man spoke.

Then Vale looked past him at the room and sighed.

“I had hoped,” he said, “that you would be more respectful of locked doors.”

Daniel’s hand found the wall behind him. The paint was cold and slick.

“You killed them.”

Vale’s expression barely shifted. “That’s such a blunt word.”

“The woman from the paper—”

“She was careless. She left her necklace behind.”

Vale stepped into the room and closed the door, leaving only the two of them beneath the flickering bulb.

Daniel’s eyes moved toward the stairs.

Vale noticed.

“You won’t make it,” he said.

The words were calm, almost apologetic. That was the worst part.

Daniel looked again at the shelves, at the photographs, at the boxes arranged like gifts. He thought of all the times he had waved to Vale while taking out the trash. All the times he had heard footsteps next door after midnight. All the times Vale had smiled and asked whether Daniel was sleeping well.

Then he noticed the furnace.

Its control panel was old, but beside it sat a newer device: a red emergency switch connected to an alarm system. Daniel had seen the same model on a television commercial. Fire suppression. Whole-house alert.

His gaze lingered on it for half a second.

Vale followed his eyes.

Daniel moved first.

He seized the nearest box and hurled it at the light. Glass shattered. The bulb went out, plunging the room into darkness.

Vale lunged.

Daniel ducked, felt something slice across his shoulder, and slammed into the workbench. Instruments clattered to the floor. He reached blindly for the wall, found the red switch, and pulled it down.

The alarm began screaming.

Above them, every light in the house snapped on. A siren blared through the walls, loud enough to shake the shelves. Somewhere upstairs, the front door opened.

A woman shouted.

Then another voice: “Police! Hands where I can see them!”

Vale froze.

Daniel crawled toward the doorway as officers thundered down the stairs. One tackled Vale into the concrete. Another dragged Daniel away, wrapping his shoulder in a towel.

For several minutes, the basement was noise and motion—boots, shouted commands, the crash of cabinets being opened.

Then, slowly, it became quiet.

An officer stood beneath the broken bulb, staring at the room.

“Jesus,” he whispered.

Daniel looked at the mannequin one last time.

The photograph pinned beneath its throat was gone.

Vale had taken it with him when he fell.

And on the back, written in neat black ink, were four words:

**You were almost ready.**

The hotel room smelled of lemon polish, rain, and the faint metallic tang of gun oil.

Mara sat cross-legged on the carpet, a towel spread beneath her knees. She held a pistol in one hand and ran a cloth along its slide with the patient attention of someone polishing silverware.

Across from her, Felix had dismantled a knife down to its smallest practical parts. He arranged them in a neat row on the desk, beside the room-service menu and a bowl of untouched mints.

“You know what I miss?” he said.

Mara glanced up. “Competent employers?”

“Besides that.”

“Good coffee?”

“Old-fashioned work.”

She raised an eyebrow. “You’re twenty-eight.”

“Exactly. I grew up in the wrong era.”

Mara clicked the pistol back together. “You’ve been watching those historical dramas again.”

“They had style. Poison in the wine. A locked room. A tragic final speech.” Felix lifted the knife handle and inspected it for dust. “Now everything is cameras and spreadsheets.”

“You say that as if you don’t keep spreadsheets.”

“I keep records. There’s a difference.”

“There really isn’t.”

He smiled and reached for a cloth. “My favorite is still poison.”

“Of course it is.”

“It’s elegant. Quiet. Personal, if you do it properly.”

“Poison is unreliable.”

“So are people. That’s part of the charm.”

Mara leaned back against the bed. Outside, tires hissed along the wet street six floors below. The television played silently, showing a news anchor gesturing beneath a red banner.

“My favorite,” she said, “is the one that looks like an accident.”

Felix paused. “That’s not a method. That’s a category.”

“It’s a philosophy.”

“You would say that.”

“No witnesses. No dramatic cleanup. Everyone gets to keep their comforting story.” She folded the cloth and began cleaning the pistol’s grip. “Man slips. Woman wanders into traffic. Executive discovers the consequences of underestimating gravity.”

“Gravity,” Felix said. “The assassin’s oldest accomplice.”

“Reliable. Patient. Never asks for a bonus.”

He considered this while reassembling the knife. “I prefer drowning.”

“Too messy.”

“Only if you’re bad at it.”

Mara gave him a flat look.

Felix sighed. “Fine. Too messy for hotels.”

“That’s better.”

He fitted the blade into its handle and tested the hinge. “There’s something honest about it, though. No theatrics. Just silence and water.”

“You’re becoming sentimental.”

“I’m appreciating atmosphere.”

“You once complained that a target’s apartment had ‘the wrong kind of curtains.’”

“They did.”

“They were beige.”

“Exactly.”

Mara finished with the pistol and set it on the towel. “My second favorite is a fall.”

“Your second favorite is gravity?”

“My second favorite is letting someone make the mistake themselves.”

Felix nodded slowly. “That’s less a method than a personality assessment.”

“The best jobs are.”

For a moment, only the rain spoke.

Then Felix picked up the room-service menu. “What do you think our target prefers?”

“His last meal?”

“His method of death.”

Mara looked toward the closed bathroom door, then at the expensive painting above the minibar—a blue vase rendered in several hundred dollars’ worth of melancholy.

“He strikes me as a man who would choose something elaborate,” she said.

“Like?”

“Something involving a secret passage, a family curse, and a woman in a red dress.”

Felix snorted. “That’s three methods.”

“He has the budget.”

A soft buzz came from Mara’s phone.

She checked the message and stood.

Felix slipped the cleaned knife into its sheath. “Time?”

“Now.”

He placed the last pistol part into its socket and snapped the case shut. “Shame. We never settled the question.”

“What question?”

“The best way.”

Mara opened the door. Warm hallway light spilled across the carpet.

“The best way,” she said, “is the one nobody remembers.”

Felix followed her out, leaving the weapons gleaming on the towel and the television silently announcing someone else’s tragedy.

The graveyard had forgotten the moon.

Clouds pressed low over the hills, thick and colorless, while beneath them the dead rose in rows.

At the center of the burial ground stood Veyr, the necromancer, barefoot in the frost. A circle of black salt surrounded him, though the salt did not lie still. It crawled in tiny streams, drawing and redrawing symbols that had no place in any human alphabet.

He lifted one hand.

The earth split.

A corpse clawed its way upward, its fingers slick with grave water and black mud. What remained of its face came free in pieces. Skin sagged from the cheekbones like wet parchment; one eye had collapsed entirely, leaving a hollow filled with glistening worms. The jaw hung loose, revealing teeth furred with green rot.

Veyr whispered a word.

The corpse snapped upright.

Its spine bent with a series of soft, damp pops. Tendons stretched between exposed joints. A strip of flesh peeled from its forearm and dangled there, pale and fibrous, but the dead thing did not seem to notice. It turned toward the necromancer, waiting.

Another grave opened.

Then another.

The soil heaved across the hill as if something enormous beneath it were breathing. Coffins burst apart. Bones emerged first, followed by hands, shoulders, and skulls filmed in clotted earth. Some dead were little more than skeletons draped in rotting clothes. Others came up nearly whole: soldiers with bellies split open, farmers with swollen tongues protruding between broken teeth, children whose faces had been preserved by the cold until the instant Veyr’s magic touched them.

Then they began to decay.

The spell did not restore them. It persuaded their remains to imitate life.

Rot raced across their bodies in branching stains. Skin blistered and tore. Bellies sagged as trapped gases escaped in wet sighs. Maggots spilled from the folds of their clothing and vanished into the dark beneath their ribs. Yet the corpses marched, their movements jerking and imprecise, as though invisible hands were working them from inside.

That was the wrongness of it.

No wind stirred, but the dead leaned toward Veyr.

No command was spoken, but their mouths opened together.

No lungs remained in their chests, but they inhaled.

The sound rolled over the graveyard—a thousand dry, rattling breaths drawn through ruined throats. It was not a roar, nor a groan. It was the imitation of one. A mockery assembled from remembered pieces.

Veyr smiled.

His shadow did not.

It stretched behind him in the shape of a tall, antlered thing, though nothing stood there. When he raised both arms, the shadow raised four. When he turned his head, its faceless skull remained fixed upon the graves.

The earth answered with another convulsion.

At the far edge of the cemetery, an old woman’s corpse rose from beneath a stone angel. Her hands were folded neatly over her breast, her gray hair still braided. For one heartbeat, she looked almost peaceful.

Then her eyes opened.

They were full of soil.

Her mouth formed a name.

Veyr flinched—not from fear, but annoyance—and clenched his fist. The corpse’s jaw cracked sideways. The name became a wet gargle. She joined the others.

Beyond the cemetery, the living watched from the black road: villagers, deserters, men who had come armed with torches and found that fire offered little comfort against an army that had already died once.

The dead gathered in silence.

Some limped. Some crawled. One dragged its own severed leg behind it by the ankle. A knight in rusted armor marched with half his chest missing, a blue flame burning where his heart had been. Wherever the flame cast its light, the grass withered and bent away.

Veyr stepped to the front of his army.

The dead followed.

Their feet sank into the mud, but left no footprints. Their shadows pointed in different directions. And as they passed beneath the ruined gate, every corpse turned its head toward the village—not together, not in unison, but one after another, as if something deep inside each of them had noticed the same scent.

The villagers began to pray.

The dead began to remember how to smile.

The alley smelled of rain, rust, and old garbage. The recruit stood beneath a flickering security light while the gang leaders formed a half-circle around him, blocking every exit.

“Everybody says they’re loyal,” the leader said. “Words don’t mean anything.”

The victim was forced to his knees nearby, bruised and terrified. The recruit knew him—an older man from the neighborhood who had once helped his family. That was the point. The gang wanted the choice to hurt.

A knife was pressed into the recruit’s hand. Around him, the others muttered insults and threats, daring him to hesitate. One leader leaned close and whispered that refusing would make him the next example. Another reminded him that the gang knew where his sister went to school. Their pressure was constant, turning fear into a kind of tunnel vision.

When the recruit finally struck, the group erupted—not in celebration, but in approval, as if his violence had erased the last piece of himself that might have resisted them. The leaders clapped him on the shoulder and called him family. Behind them, the wounded man groaned on the pavement.

The recruit stared at the blood on his hands and understood the truth: the initiation was not about proving loyalty. It was about making him believe there was no way back.

I had chosen the soup because it encouraged patience.

It arrived steaming in white bowls, fragrant with thyme and roasted garlic, and my victim lifted the first spoonful without suspicion. Across the table, Lord Veylan was explaining why the northern provinces would never rebel.

“People fear change,” he said. “That is all. Give them bread, give them music, and they will remain loyal.”

I smiled and dipped my spoon into my own untouched bowl.

He took another mouthful.

At first, nothing changed. That was the trouble with waiting: the body kept its secrets. Veylan talked, laughed, and tore a piece of bread in half. Candlelight warmed his face. The gold ring on his right hand flashed whenever he gestured.

Then he paused.

Only for a breath.

His spoon hovered above the bowl. He blinked, as though he had lost the thread of his own argument.

“Of course,” he continued. “There are always—”

He swallowed.

The color had begun to leave him.

“Always?” I prompted.

“Always… exceptions.”

His voice sounded slightly farther away. He reached for his wine, but his fingers closed around the stem of the glass with unusual care. The first attempt failed. The glass rattled against the table. He laughed at himself.

“Too much wine,” he said.

He had not drunk enough to blame the wine.

I watched a faint sheen gather at his temples. He dabbed it with his napkin, then pressed the cloth to his mouth. His breathing had changed—not yet labored, but deliberate, as if each breath required consideration.

The sea was black beneath the *Marauder’s Moon*, its waves lifting and dropping the ship like a restless beast. Lanterns swung from the rigging, painting the deck in strips of yellow light.

At the bow, a single plank jutted over the rail.

Elias Vane stood at its end with his wrists bound behind him. The wind clawed at his shirt, and far below, the water churned with pale flashes—shark bellies turning beneath the moon.

Captain Rook drew his cutlass and rested its tip between Elias’s shoulder blades.

“You were warned,” he said.

“I was starving,” Elias answered, though his voice shook. “Half the crew was starving.”

A murmur moved through the pirates. Some looked away. Others stared hungrily toward the sea.

Rook’s expression did not change. “You raised a blade against your captain.”

“I raised it against a tyrant.”

The captain stepped closer. “Then you’ll die proving your courage.”

He struck Elias between the shoulders.

The mutineer stumbled forward. His boot slid across the wet plank, and for one terrible instant he windmilled his arms, bound hands useless behind him. He looked back at the deck—the faces, the lanterns, the captain’s cold eyes—and then down.

The sharks were closer now.

Their fins cut the surface in widening circles. One opened its mouth, revealing rows of teeth that gleamed like broken glass.

Elias dropped to his knees.

“Please,” he gasped.

Rook kicked the plank.

Elias plunged into the darkness.

The sea closed over him with a hard splash. For a heartbeat, nothing moved but the waves. Then he surfaced, screaming, and thrashed toward the ship.

“Pull me up!” he cried. “Captain!”

A shape slid beneath him.

The water erupted.

A shark struck from below, lifting Elias halfway out of the sea. Its jaws clamped around his thigh, and his scream became a raw, strangled howl. Red spread through the black water as the animal twisted, dragging him beneath the surface.

The crew watched in silence.

Elias reappeared several yards away, flailing with one arm. His face was white with terror. He tried to swim, but one leg hung uselessly behind him, trailing a dark ribbon. More fins converged.

“No!” he screamed. “No, no—help me!”

Another shark slammed into his side. Its teeth tore through cloth and flesh, spinning him like a rag in the foam. Blood burst across the waves. Elias vanished beneath a boiling mass of gray backs and snapping jaws.

For a moment, his hand broke the surface.

His fingers opened and closed.

Then a final surge swallowed him.

The sea settled slowly, leaving only scraps of cloth and a widening stain that the tide pulled apart.

No one spoke.

Captain Rook sheathed his cutlass and turned toward the crew.

“Let that be the fate of every man who mistakes hunger for mutiny.”

Below them, the sharks circled in the moonlit water, waiting for whatever the sea had not yet claimed.

At first, Elias heard the knocking only at night.

Three slow knocks against the bedroom door.

Not loud. Not urgent. Almost polite.

He would lie rigid beneath the blankets, staring into the darkness, and wait for them to stop. They always did. After a minute, sometimes two, silence returned to the house.

By morning, he convinced himself it had been the pipes.

On the seventh night, a voice came with the knocking.

“Elias.”

He stopped breathing.

The voice was soft, hoarse, and unmistakable.

Mara.

He had buried her beneath the old ash tree at the edge of the property. He had packed the dirt down with the heel of his boot and scattered dead leaves over the disturbed ground. He had burned the clothes he wore that night and scrubbed his hands until the skin split across his knuckles.

No one knew.

No one except Mara.

“Elias,” the voice whispered again.

The doorknob began to turn.

He sprang from the bed and seized the handle, holding it shut with both hands. The wood shuddered beneath his grip. On the other side, something dragged a fingernail down the door.

Slowly.

Patiently.

“I’m sorry,” he breathed.

The scratching stopped.

A moment later, Mara laughed.

He stumbled backward. The room seemed to tilt, the walls leaning inward as though the house itself were listening. He looked toward the mirror above the dresser and saw her standing behind him.

Her throat was dark with bruises.

Her hair hung wet against her face.

One eye stared at him, pale and clouded. The other was the same warm brown he remembered from the last time she had looked at him and asked, *Why?*

Elias spun around.

There was no one there.

In the mirror, she remained.

He smashed it with the lamp.

The next morning, he found muddy footprints in the hallway.

They began at the front door and ended beside his bed.

He scrubbed them away until the floorboards gleamed. By noon, he had convinced himself they were his own. By evening, he had forgotten whether he had gone outside.

The house changed after that.

Doors stood open when he knew he had closed them. The kitchen tap ran red for several minutes before becoming water again. He heard Mara moving through the rooms, humming the tune she used to sing while washing dishes. Sometimes he saw her in the corner of his vision: a pale figure slipping behind a doorway, a hand resting on the banister, a face reflected in the black screen of the television.

Whenever he turned to look, she vanished.

Whenever he looked away, she came closer.

He stopped sleeping.

On the fourth sleepless night, he found her sitting at the kitchen table.

Moonlight passed through her.

The chair beneath her did not creak.

“You shouldn’t be here,” Elias said.

Mara tilted her head. “Neither should I.”

Her mouth opened too far when she smiled.

He backed into the counter. “I didn’t mean to.”

“You brought the shovel.”

“I was angry.”

“You locked the door.”

“I thought you would tell them.”

“You watched me stop breathing.”

Elias clapped his hands over his ears, but her voice continued inside his skull.

He saw it again—the woods, the rain, Mara on her knees in the mud. He saw the stone in his hand. Saw it rise. Saw it fall.

Then the memory changed.

Mara became his mother.

Then his father.

Then Elias himself, kneeling beneath the ash tree, pleading for mercy while another Elias stood over him with the stone.

He screamed and overturned the table.

When he looked up, every chair in the kitchen was occupied.

Mara sat in the first.

The others held versions of her: Mara as a child, Mara with a broken neck, Mara with her skull crushed inward, Mara smiling calmly with dirt packed beneath her fingernails.

All of them watched him.

All of them whispered his name.

Elias fled into the hall. The walls were covered in writing.

Not ink. Not blood.

His own handwriting, carved into the plaster with a kitchen knife.

**I AM SORRY.**

**I AM SORRY.**

**I AM SORRY.**

The words overlapped until they became a black, crawling mass.

At the end of the hall, Mara stood beneath the dead lightbulb.

She looked almost alive now.

That was worse.

“You said no one would find me,” she murmured.

Elias shook his head. “I didn’t tell anyone.”

“You told yourself.”

The floorboards groaned beneath him.

From somewhere beneath the house came the muffled sound of knocking.

Three slow knocks.

Then three more.

Elias stared at the floor.

The ash tree had no roots beneath the house. He knew that. He had measured the distance himself.

Still, something scraped beneath the boards.

A fingernail.

Then another.

Then many.

Mara stepped closer. Her feet did not touch the floor.

“You can hear them,” she said.

“Who?”

“The dead.”

The boards split.

Black fingers pushed through the gap.

Elias fell backward, sobbing, as the floor burst apart and the smell of wet earth filled the hall. Shapes crawled from the darkness—faceless figures in torn clothes, their hands swollen and muddy. He recognized some of them. People he had lied to. People he had betrayed. People whose names he had forgotten.

Mara stood among them.

She reached for his face.

Her fingers were cold as grave dirt.

“Don’t be afraid,” she whispered.

Elias laughed then—a thin, broken sound that rose into a shriek.

“I’m not afraid.”

Mara’s thumb brushed his cheek.

“No,” she said. “You’re relieved.”

In the morning, the neighbors found the front door wide open.

Elias was gone.

They searched the house, the road, and the fields beyond it. Near the ash tree, they discovered a patch of freshly turned earth.

No body.

Only a shovel lying in the mud.

And beneath the tree, carved into the bark in deep, frantic letters:

**SHE KNOWS WHERE I AM.**

The rain had polished the alley slick, but it couldn’t wash the stink out of it. Rain never could. It only moved the filth around, gave the city a clean face while the rot crawled underneath.

He lay beneath the fire escape, one hand curled toward the gutter as if he’d been trying to climb out of the world. The other was buried in his coat. His eyes stared at the brick wall, wide and cloudy, catching the red pulse of the patrol car’s lights. They looked like two dead windows in a condemned building.

I’d seen plenty of bodies. The city made them the way a factory makes bolts—cold, regular, and without asking who needed them. But this one had been handled with patience. Whoever did it hadn’t been angry. Anger is quick. This was bookkeeping.

A thin stream of blood threaded through the cracks in the pavement, joining the rainwater and cigarette ash. It ran toward the storm drain, black and shining, like the city was sipping through a straw. Somewhere below us, the sewers were swallowing another secret.

I crouched beside him. His face had already started to lose its argument with death. Color drained from it, leaving the gray of old plaster, the kind you find in buildings where the tenants have moved out but the mold stayed behind. His mouth hung open, as if the last thing he’d seen had been too large to name.

The alley smelled of wet brick, gasoline, and the sweet edge of decay. The whole neighborhood smelled that way if you knew how to breathe: perfume over garbage, hot bread over sewage, money over fear. The city was a carcass in a good suit, and every night the rats held another banquet.

“Name?” the uniform asked.

I looked at the dead man’s fingers. There was grime beneath the nails and a pale crescent of skin where a ring had been removed. Not stolen. Removed. Whoever had done this wanted something more valuable than gold.

“Not yet,” I said.

The uniform frowned. He wanted a name to put on a form, a box to close, a line to draw beneath the evening. But murder didn’t work that way. It seeped. It spread through the streets like damp through a basement wall. By morning, somebody would be lying about where they’d been. By noon, somebody else would be missing. By nightfall, the city would have built another floor over the truth.

I stood, my knees complaining like old pipes.

The rain kept falling.

results.model_response_html:
The rain had polished the alley slick, but it couldn’t wash the stink out of it. Rain never could. It only moved the filth around, gave the city a clean face while the rot crawled underneath.

He lay beneath the fire escape, one hand curled toward the gutter as if he’d been trying to climb out of the world. The other was buried in his coat. His eyes stared at the brick wall, wide and cloudy, catching the red pulse of the patrol car’s lights. They looked like two dead windows in a condemned building.

I’d seen plenty of bodies. The city made them the way a factory makes bolts—cold, regular, and without asking who needed them. But this one had been handled with patience. Whoever did it hadn’t been angry. Anger is quick. This was bookkeeping.

A thin stream of blood threaded through the cracks in the pavement, joining the rainwater and cigarette ash. It ran toward the storm drain, black and shining, like the city was sipping through a straw. Somewhere below us, the sewers were swallowing another secret.

I crouched beside him. His face had already started to lose its argument with death. Color drained from it, leaving the gray of old plaster, the kind you find in buildings where the tenants have moved out but the mold stayed behind. His mouth hung open, as if the last thing he’d seen had been too large to name.

The alley smelled of wet brick, gasoline, and the sweet edge of decay. The whole neighborhood smelled that way if you knew how to breathe: perfume over garbage, hot bread over sewage, money over fear. The city was a carcass in a good suit, and every night the rats held another banquet.

“Name?” the uniform asked.

I looked at the dead man’s fingers. There was grime beneath the nails and a pale crescent of skin where a ring had been removed. Not stolen. Removed. Whoever had done this wanted something more valuable than gold.

“Not yet,” I said.

The uniform frowned. He wanted a name to put on a form, a box to close, a line to draw beneath the evening. But murder didn’t work that way. It seeped. It spread through the streets like damp through a basement wall. By morning, somebody would be lying about where they’d been. By noon, somebody else would be missing. By nightfall, the city would have built another floor over the truth.

I stood, my knees complaining like old pipes.

The rain kept falling.

It tapped on the metal fire escape, whispered through the trash, and gathered around the body in widening circles—like the whole rotten town was leaning closer to listen.

The city sirens began at dusk.

They rolled through the abandoned financial district in slow, mournful waves, stirring dust from the broken windows and sending flocks of gray birds spiraling into the violet sky. Every screen still worked, though most of the buildings did not. Across walls and towers, the same message flickered:

**THE HUNT IS LIVE.  
FORTY-EIGHT MINUTES REMAIN.  
RUN WELL.**

Mara ran beneath the screens.

Her shoes slapped the flooded pavement. One sleeve of her coat had torn away, and blood from a cut above her eyebrow blurred one eye. Behind her, somewhere in the maze of alleys, came the measured chime of a hunter’s bell.

Not a human bell. A signal.

Three notes. Pause. Three notes.

It meant the hunter had entered the district.

Mara stumbled past a toppled transit kiosk and caught herself against a concrete pillar. Her breath shook in her lungs. The collar around her throat pulsed once, tightening just enough to remind her it was there.

Every runner wore one. The collar broadcast their location, measured their heart rate, and recorded the final moment for the viewers at home. If a runner reached one of the safe gates before the timer expired, the collar unlocked.

If not, the hunter claimed the prize.

A red drone drifted overhead, its camera eye swiveling toward her.

Mara froze.

The drone flashed her face onto the nearest building. A white outline surrounded her body. Somewhere beyond the walls, spectators began to cheer.

Then the bell sounded again.

Three notes.

Closer.

She broke into a side street, running toward the old opera house. Its doors had been chained shut for years, but she knew about the service entrance in the rear. Inside, the maze of backstage corridors might give her enough time to lose him.

The city had once been built for millions. Now it existed to entertain them.

Mara reached the alley behind the opera house and found the door hanging open.

Too open.

She slowed.

The bell did not sound again.

That was worse.

She stepped inside.

The corridor smelled of wet stone and old electricity. Torn curtains hung from the ceiling like flayed banners. Somewhere, water dripped with maddening regularity.

A shadow moved at the far end.

Mara turned to run, but a wire snapped tight around her ankle.

She hit the floor hard.

The air left her. Her palms skidded over grit. She clawed for the wire, but it had already cinched into a steel loop. The collar at her throat flashed amber.

**RUNNER RESTRAINED.**

The message appeared on every surviving screen in the city.

Applause erupted from hidden speakers.

Mara twisted onto her back.

The hunter stepped into the corridor.

He wore a dark coat fitted with armored plates, polished boots, and a mirrored mask that reflected the red light of the drones. A rifle hung at his side, unused. The Games Commission preferred close captures. It made for better viewing.

In one gloved hand, he carried a length of silver chain.

“You made it farther than the odds predicted,” he said.

His voice had been altered by the mask—low, almost gentle.

Mara pulled against the snare. “Go to hell.”

The hunter tilted his head, as if considering the possibility.

Behind him, a drone projected the countdown onto the wall.

**00:17:09**

The hunter walked closer.

Mara’s fingers found the small blade hidden inside her boot. She drew it and slashed at the wire. Sparks burst from the trap. The hunter moved faster than she expected. He kicked the knife away and caught her wrist, pinning it to the floor.

The crowd roared.

“Careful,” he said. “They dislike damaged prizes.”

Mara stared up at the mirrored mask. In it, she saw herself: pale, filthy, trapped.

She spat in his face.

For a moment, the corridor went quiet except for the rain tapping through the ruined roof.

Then the hunter wiped the mask with one finger.

“Prize condition acceptable,” he said.

He pressed a metal seal against the collar at her throat. It clicked into place. The amber light changed to white.

The screens updated:

**HUNT COMPLETE.  
PRIZE CLAIMED.**

A narrow compartment opened in the hunter’s belt. Inside lay a row of small black tags, each engraved with a name and a date.

He removed an empty one.

Mara fought until the chain locked around her wrists. She fought as he dragged her upright. She fought while the drones descended, their lenses bright and hungry.

The hunter held the tag to the collar.

A spark jumped between them.

Her name appeared in white letters.

**MARA VALE — CAPTURED BY HUNTER 19**

The city cheered again.

The hunter closed his fist around the tag and turned toward the waiting cameras, claiming his prize beneath the dying lights of the opera house.

Mara looked past him, through the broken doorway, toward the distant safe gate glowing blue in the rain.

The timer kept counting down.

And somewhere in the crowd, someone began to chant her name.

The rain had turned the trench into a narrow ditch of black water.

Private Elias Mercer crouched beneath the sagging duckboards, his hands wrapped around the wooden handle of his entrenching shovel. The rifle he had carried into the line was gone—lost somewhere in the churned mud when the bombardment began. Around him, men shouted through the smoke. Some called for ammunition. Others called for their mothers.

Then the Germans came over the parapet.

They appeared as shadows first: boots slipping on the wet sandbags, bayonets flashing pale in the flare light. One of them landed directly in front of Elias.

For a second, neither man moved.

The German was young. Younger than Elias had expected. His face was streaked with mud, and a strip of cloth was tied around his left hand. He held a short rifle with its bayonet fixed, but the weapon had caught in the wire behind him. He tugged at it once, swore, and looked up.

His eyes met Elias’s.

There was no hatred in them. Only alarm.

The trench filled with noise. A shell burst somewhere beyond the parapet, and the earth trembled beneath their boots. Elias saw the German wrench his rifle free.

He swung the shovel.

The blade struck the side of the man’s helmet with a hard, ringing crack. The German staggered but did not fall. Elias felt the impact travel through his arms. He swung again, this time without aiming, and the shovel caught the man across the cheek.

The face opened beneath the blow.

The German collapsed against the trench wall, sliding down into the mud. His rifle clattered between them. Elias stood over him, breathing through his teeth, unable to understand what he had done or what he was still supposed to do.

The man moved.

His hand reached toward the fallen rifle.

Elias’s body acted before his mind could catch up. He drove the shovel downward.

There was a wet resistance, then a sudden release.

The German’s fingers twitched once and went still.

For a moment, the battle vanished. Elias heard only the rain tapping against his helmet. He stared at the shovel. Its blade was buried in the man’s chest, and the wooden haft quivered beneath his hands.

He let go.

Someone shoved past him, firing over the parapet. Another soldier yelled that the Germans were falling back. Elias barely heard them. He looked down at the dead man’s face.

The helmet had rolled away. Without it, the man looked impossibly ordinary. A lock of fair hair lay plastered against his forehead. His mouth was slightly open, as if he had been about to say something.

Elias knelt.

He did not know why. Perhaps he meant to pull the shovel free. Perhaps he meant to help. His hand reached toward the man’s shoulder and stopped just above it.

The torn cloth around the left hand had come loose. Beneath it, the fingers were small and clean despite the mud. A wedding ring gleamed on one of them.

Elias began to shake.

He had imagined killing before. Every soldier did, though no one admitted it. In his imagination, the enemy was faceless—a gray uniform, a helmet, a shape behind smoke. Something distant enough to hate. But this man had a ring. He had eyes. He had looked frightened.

He had been alive less than a minute ago.

Elias stumbled backward until his shoulders struck the trench wall. He pressed both hands over his mouth. The smell of mud, cordite, and blood filled his nose. He retched into the water at his feet, bringing up nothing but bile.

A sergeant grabbed him by the collar.

“Mercer! Get that shovel out. We need the trench cleared.”

Elias stared at him.

“What?”

“The shovel.” The sergeant pointed. “Move.”

Elias looked down again. The handle was still lodged in the German’s body.

He reached for it, but his fingers would not close. The sergeant cursed, seized the haft himself, and pulled. The blade came free with a sucking sound. Elias flinched as though he had been struck.

The sergeant thrust the shovel back at him.

“Hold it.”

Elias did.

He spent the rest of the night carrying the weapon without using it. He could feel its weight in every step. Mud clung to the blade. Something darker ran in a thin line along its edge, disappearing beneath the wooden socket.

When dawn came, the trench was quiet except for the distant guns.

Elias sat beneath the parapet and tried to clean the shovel with a rag. He scrubbed until the metal shone, then scrubbed harder. The rag tore. His hands were raw. Still he continued, staring at the stain that would not leave.

At last, he threw the shovel into the mud.

A few feet away, the German’s body lay where it had fallen. Someone had covered the face with a torn sandbag, but one hand remained exposed.

The ring was gone.

Elias wondered who had taken it, and whether the thief had known that somewhere across the lines, perhaps in a small house with a garden, someone was waiting for the man to come home.

The thought settled inside him like a second wound.

Years later, Elias would forget battles, dates, and the names of men who had shared his dugout. He would forget the sound of particular guns.

He would never forget the moment the German looked at him.

Not because the man had been his enemy.

Because, for one terrible instant, they had both understood that neither of them wanted to die.

The square had been built for this.

Its stones sloped gently toward a drain at the center, and every building around it carried the same black-and-gold banner: **ORDER IS MERCY**. On ordinary days, the square hosted markets and military bands. On sentencing days, the market stalls were pushed back, and a wooden platform was raised beneath the clock tower.

By noon, the crowd had filled every space.

Mara stood between her mother and a fishmonger who had brought his youngest daughter to watch. The girl clutched a paper cone of sugared nuts and kept asking when the play would begin.

“It isn’t a play,” the fishmonger muttered.

His voice held the same flatness as everyone else’s. People came because attendance was recorded. They came because absence invited questions. They came because, after years of executions for unlicensed trading, insulting a magistrate, missing a work quota, and taking food without paying, it had become easier to stand among the crowd than to stand apart from it.

The platform doors opened.

A boy was led out between two officers.

He could not have been older than sixteen. His prison shirt hung from narrow shoulders, and one sleeve had been mended with blue thread. His hair had been shaved close, but a dark curl had escaped near his ear. He looked at the crowd as if searching for a familiar face.

Mara saw one.

A woman near the fountain made a sound like a breath caught in a locked room. She stepped forward, then stopped when the officer beside her placed a hand on his baton.

“Eli,” she whispered.

The boy heard her. His face changed—not with fear, exactly, but recognition. His mouth opened.

“Ma—”

The crier struck the butt of his staff against the platform.

“Elias Venn,” he announced, “convicted under the Bread Security Act for theft of one municipal loaf.”

A few people shifted uncomfortably.

One loaf.

The words seemed absurdly small beneath the tower, smaller than the banners, smaller than the rifles, smaller than the silence gathering over the square.

The crier continued. “The sentence is execution, that the appetite of one may not become the hunger of many.”

An old man near Mara gave a bitter laugh. “There are warehouses full of bread.”

His wife seized his sleeve. “Be quiet.”

A child began to cry. Her mother pressed the sugared-nut cone into her hands and turned the girl’s face against her coat. The fishmonger stared at the platform, jaw working. Someone in the back shouted, “Law is law!”

The chant was taken up unevenly.

“Law is law.”

A few voices joined.

“Law is law.”

Most did not.

Elias was made to kneel. His mother pushed through the crowd then, sobbing openly. Two officers caught her before she reached the steps. She fought them with surprising strength, calling her son’s name again and again until the sound broke into something hoarse.

Mara felt her mother’s fingers close around her wrist.

“Don’t look,” she said.

But Mara looked.

Not at the officials. Not at the soldiers. At the crowd.

She saw a baker staring at his hands, flour still caught beneath his fingernails. She saw a woman quietly remove a crust from her pocket and hide it beneath her shawl. She saw the fishmonger’s daughter peeking between her mother’s skirts, confused by the grown-ups’ terror. She saw men in government caps watching with stern faces, though one of them had gone pale.

The square waited for obedience to feel like righteousness.

When the mechanism was activated, there was no dramatic sound—only a sharp click swallowed by the bells above them.

Elias disappeared from view.

His mother screamed.

The crowd flinched as one body. Some cried out. Some bowed their heads. One man vomited against the fountain. Others began clapping because the guards were watching, because the officials were watching, because everyone was watching everyone else.

Mara did not clap.

Around her, the applause spread and faltered, spread and faltered, until it sounded less like approval than rain striking a thousand locked doors.

The crier raised his staff again.

“Let this be remembered,” he called.

But years later, Mara would remember something else: not the decree, nor the banners, nor the execution itself.

She would remember the boy looking into the crowd, still expecting someone to help.

He could not have been older than sixteen. His prison shirt hung from narrow shoulders, and one sleeve had been mended with blue thread. His hair had been shaved close, but a dark curl had escaped near his ear. He looked at the crowd as if searching for a familiar face.

Mara saw one.

A woman near the fountain made a sound like a breath caught in a locked room. She stepped forward, then stopped when the officer beside her placed a hand on his baton.

“Eli,” she whispered.

The boy heard her. His face changed—not with fear, exactly, but recognition. His mouth opened.

“Ma—”

The crier struck the butt of his staff against the platform.

“Elias Venn,” he announced, “convicted under the Bread Security Act for theft of one municipal loaf.”

A few people shifted uncomfortably.

One loaf.

The words seemed absurdly small beneath the tower, smaller than the banners, smaller than the rifles, smaller than the silence gathering over the square.

The crier continued. “The sentence is execution, that the appetite of one may not become the hunger of many.”

An old man near Mara gave a bitter laugh. “There are warehouses full of bread.”

His wife seized his sleeve. “Be quiet.”

A child began to cry. Her mother pressed the sugared-nut cone into her hands and turned the girl’s face against her coat. The fishmonger stared at the platform, jaw working. Someone in the back shouted, “Law is law!”

The chant was taken up unevenly.

“Law is law.”

A few voices joined.

“Law is law.”

Most did not.

Elias was made to kneel. His mother pushed through the crowd then, sobbing openly. Two officers caught her before she reached the steps. She fought them with surprising strength, calling her son’s name again and again until the sound broke into something hoarse.

Mara felt her mother’s fingers close around her wrist.

“Don’t look,” she said.

But Mara looked.

Not at the officials. Not at the soldiers. At the crowd.

She saw a baker staring at his hands, flour still caught beneath his fingernails. She saw a woman quietly remove a crust from her pocket and hide it beneath her shawl. She saw the fishmonger’s daughter peeking between her mother’s skirts, confused by the grown-ups’ terror. She saw men in government caps watching with stern faces, though one of them had gone pale.

The square waited for obedience to feel like righteousness.

When the mechanism was activated, there was no dramatic sound—only a sharp click swallowed by the bells above them.

Elias disappeared from view.

His mother screamed.

The crowd flinched as one body. Some cried out. Some bowed their heads. One man vomited against the fountain. Others began clapping because the guards were watching, because the officials were watching, because everyone was watching everyone else.

Mara did not clap.

Around her, the applause spread and faltered, spread and faltered, until it sounded less like approval than rain striking a thousand locked doors.

The crier raised his staff again.

“Let this be remembered,” he called.

But years later, Mara would remember something else: not the decree, nor the banners, nor the execution itself.

She would remember the boy looking into the crowd, still expecting someone to help.

The debt collector shut the apartment door behind him and slid the bolt home.

The man on the floor tried to push himself backward, palms slipping on the worn linoleum. “I told you, I need another week.”

“You had another week.”

The collector carried the bat loosely in one hand. It was scarred and darkened at the barrel, more tool than weapon now. He looked at the man’s shaking fingers, then at the envelope of unpaid bills scattered near the radiator.

“Please.”

The first strike landed below the knee.

The sound was blunt and terrible—a heavy *crack* followed by the clatter of the bat against the floor. The man’s scream tore out of him before he seemed to understand what had happened. His hands flew to his leg, but the collector caught his shoulder and shoved him flat.

“Don’t touch it.”

The man gasped through clenched teeth. His face had gone gray. Sweat sprang across his forehead as his leg lay twisted at an angle it had never been meant to take.

“One payment,” the collector said. “That’s all you had to make.”

The man begged then. Not words at first, just ragged sounds, breath scraping in and out of his throat. He promised money, names, favors—anything. The collector waited until the promises ran out.

Then he raised the bat again.

The second blow struck the other leg.

A dull, wet *thud*. A sharper crack underneath it.

The man’s body jerked. His scream collapsed into a strangled howl, and he clawed at the floorboards until his fingernails split. For a moment he couldn’t breathe. The room narrowed to the fluorescent buzz overhead, the hot pulse of pain swallowing everything else.

The collector leaned on the bat and watched him tremble.

“Next time,” he said, “you pay before I come back.”

He left the bat on the table.

The door opened, then closed. Footsteps descended the stairwell, unhurried.

On the floor, the man tried to crawl toward the phone. Each movement sent lightning through both legs. He made it six inches before the pain overwhelmed him, and he collapsed beside the scattered bills, sobbing into the linoleum while the dial tone waited somewhere just beyond his reach.
